The evaluation context of each item Each item is evaluated with its own values in the IEvaluationContext, while the materialized collections are shared with the whole evaluation.

A collection that the caller passes as the expected value, e.g. the titles a playlist must contain, can also be a query that may only be enumerated once. Enumerate it only once per evaluation: copy it at the start of IsMetBy unless it already is a collection, and use only the copy afterwards, also for the failure message: public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context) { Actual = actual; ICollection<string> titles = expected as ICollection<string> ?? expected.ToArray(); if (actual is not null) { _missingTitles = titles .Except(context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual).Select(track => track.Title)) .ToList(); Outcome = _missingTitles.Count == 0 ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } The subject itself still goes through UseMaterializedEnumerable, so that it is shared with the other expectations on it, while the expected collection belongs to your constraint alone.

To compare items with an expected collection like the collection IsEqualTo does, get a matcher from CollectionMatchOptions and let VerifyItems run it over the items. It returns the outcome together with the failure text of IsEqualTo, e.g. it lacked 1 of 2 expected items: "Outro", so the caller's choice of InAnyOrder(), IgnoringDuplicates() or IgnoringCase() applies to your expectation as well: public static StringCollectionMatchResult<IEnumerable<Track>, IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?>> HasTitles( this IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?> subject, params string[] expected) { OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> options = new(StringEqualityOptions.Default); OptionsHolder<CollectionMatchOptions> matchOptions = new(CollectionMatchOptions.Default); return new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new HasTitlesConstraint(it, grammars, expected, options, matchOptions)), subject, options, matchOptions); } private sealed class HasTitlesConstraint( string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, string[] expected, IReadOnlyOptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> options, IReadOnlyOptionsHolder<CollectionMatchOptions> matchOptions) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<IEnumerable<Track>>(it, grammars), IAsyncContextConstraint<IEnumerable<Track>?> { private string? _failure; public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { Actual = actual; _failure = null; foreach (string title in expected) { options.Value.ValidateExpected(title, nameof(expected)); } if (actual is null) { Outcome = Outcome.Failure; return this; } IEnumerable<string?> titles = context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual).Select(track => track.Title); (Outcome, _failure) = await matchOptions.Value.GetCollectionMatcher<string?, string?>(expected) .VerifyItems(It, titles, options.Value.ForEvaluation(context, cancellationToken), cancellationToken); return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("has titles that ").Append(matchOptions.Value.GetExpectation( Formatter.Format(expected, FormattingOptions.SingleLine) + options.Value, ExpectationGrammars.Plural)); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(_failure); protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("has titles that ").Append(matchOptions.Value.GetExpectation( Formatter.Format(expected, FormattingOptions.SingleLine) + options.Value, ExpectationGrammars.Plural | ExpectationGrammars.Negated)); protected override void AppendNegatedResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" did"); } await That(tracks).HasTitles("Intro", "Outro").InAnyOrder() then fails with e.g. but it contained item "Bonus" at index 1 that was not expected. Validate every expected item with ValidateExpected(item, nameof(expected)) of the options before you look at the subject, as above, so that an item the options cannot use, e.g. an invalid regex pattern after AsRegex(), throws whichever items the subject has. A custom match type decides which items it rejects. How the items are verified The items are verified one by one until the matcher fails or is determined, e.g. once all expected items of a containment are found, and then completed. While the matcher and the comparison answer synchronously, the result completes synchronously, too. An exception while the items are enumerated fails the expectation like one of the code of the caller. The outcome stays Undecided when the CancellationToken is canceled before all items are read from their source. A collection that is complete in memory, e.g. an array, is verified completely. VerifyItems takes an IEnumerable<T>, so read the items of an IAsyncEnumerable<T> into a list first.

An expectation that compares the subject with an expected value can use the comparisons of aweXpect, so that the caller chooses the comparison with the same options as for the built-in expectations, e.g. Using(comparer), Equivalent() or IgnoringCase(). Namespaces used on this page using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Formatting; using aweXpect.Options; using aweXpect.Results; using static aweXpect.Formatting.Format;

An expectation that compares the subject for equality, e.g. an IsEqualTo for your own type, adds the equality constraint of IsEqualTo with AddEqualityConstraint from aweXpect.Core.Extending. Return an ObjectEqualityResult that shares the OptionsHolder<ObjectMatchType<T>>, so that the caller can choose the comparison, e.g. with Using(comparer) or a custom match type, and the expectation and the failure read like those of IsEqualTo: public static ObjectEqualityResult<Track?, IThat<Track?>, Track?> IsEqualTo( this IThat<Track?> subject, Track? expected) { OptionsHolder<ObjectMatchType<Track?>> options = new(ObjectMatchType<Track?>.Default); return new ObjectEqualityResult<Track?, IThat<Track?>, Track?>( subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddEqualityConstraint(expected, options), subject, options); } For IsNotEqualTo, pass isNegated: true. A null subject is never equal to an expected value that is not null, whatever the comparison. To show the code of the caller instead of the formatted value, e.g. "is equivalent to expected" like IsEquivalentTo, pass the value of a [CallerArgumentExpression] parameter as expectedExpression. How the expected expression is shown Its common leading whitespace is removed, and an expected null is still shown as <null>.

IsEqualTo compares two values with Equals, unless the caller chooses another comparison, e.g. with .Equivalent(). You can offer a comparison of your own: derive from ObjectMatchType<TElement>, pass the name of your option to its base constructor and set it on the options of the result with SetMatchType(matchType), which reads that name. For example, two tracks with the same title can count as equal: public static TSelf ByTitle<TSelf, TElement>(this IObjectEqualityResult<TSelf, TElement> result) where TSelf : IObjectEqualityResult<TSelf, TElement> { result.Options.SetMatchType(new ByTitleMatchType<TElement>()); return (TSelf)result; } private sealed class ByTitleMatchType<TElement>() : ObjectMatchType<TElement>("ByTitle") { private static readonly ByTitleMatcher Matcher = new(); public override MatchPhrase Phrase { get; } = MatchPhrase.Being("titled like").WithName(" by title"); public override ObjectMatcher<TElement> ForEvaluation(MatchEnvironment environment) => Matcher; private sealed class ByTitleMatcher : ObjectMatcher<TElement, Track> { public override ValueTask<MatchResult> Match(TElement actual, Track expected) => new(MatchResult.From(actual is Track track && track.Title == expected.Title)); public override string GetFailure(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, TElement? actual, Track expected, MatchResult result, string? indentation) => $"{it}{grammars.SubjectVerb(it, " was", " were")} titled {Formatter.Format((actual as Track)?.Title)}"; } } Track track = new("Hey Jude", new TimeSpan(0, 7, 11)); await That(track).IsEqualTo(new Track("Hey Jude", new TimeSpan(0, 7, 4))).ByTitle(); ForEvaluation returns the matcher for one evaluation. A matcher without state can be shared, as above. Match decides whether two values match, and GetFailure writes the result text of a mismatch. Phrase holds the words of the comparison, from which Core writes the expectation text in every grammar, e.g. "is titled like …", "are not titled like …" or "has item titled like …". When the result text of GetFailure spans several lines, indent the lines after the first by the indentation, e.g. with FormattingOptions.Indented(indentation) for a formatted value, so that it stays aligned inside Expect.ThatAll. Override ValidateExpected(expected, parameterName) to reject an expected value that the match type cannot use, with an ArgumentException for the parameterName it receives, as neither the match type nor the options know the parameter of the expectation. For strings, derive from StringMatchType instead and set it with SetMatchType(matchType, nameof(AsTitle)) on the StringEqualityOptions, which takes the name of your option, as a string match type carries none. Declare the settings that a string match type honors in SupportedSettings: Core rejects every other one, e.g. "IgnoringCase cannot be combined with AsTitle.". The whitespace options are supported unless you leave them out. Matchers, results, phrases and string match types in detail ForEvaluation receives the context and the cancellation of the evaluation in the MatchEnvironment. ObjectMatcher<TElement, TExpected> compares with expected values of a known type, e.g. a Track, and an expected value of another type never matches. Derive from ObjectMatcher<TElement> instead when the type of the expected value varies, e.g. an anonymous object for an equivalency, and implement the generic Match<TExpected>. Match returns MatchResult.Match, MatchResult.NoMatch, or MatchResult.NotComparable(reason) for a subject that it cannot compare at all. The expectation and its negation then both fail, with the reason as the result. Like PredicateResult.FailureBothWays, the reason follows "it". Inside Whose it follows the member name instead, and in a collection "an item", so name the value in the reason as well. A comparison that finds more than the values show, e.g. the differences of two documents, returns MatchResult.NoMatchBecause(explanation) with a MatchExplanation of its own, which the default GetFailure writes. MatchWithExplanation compares for a failure message, while Match only decides, e.g. for each item of a collection; override it when explaining costs more than deciding. MatchPhrase.Being(comparison) reads "is …", MatchPhrase.Verb(singular, plural, participle) has a verb of its own, e.g. "starts with", and MatchPhrase.EqualTo is the equality, which the text of a single item may leave out, e.g. "contains 3". WithName names the match type in a short description of the options, and WithSuffix follows the expected value, e.g. " using TitleComparer". For a string match type, WithPattern(kind, noun) marks the expected value as a pattern, e.g. wildcard "Let*" for an expected item, and WithUnformattedExpected() writes it as it is instead of quoting it, e.g. a JSON document. The matcher can add contexts that explain a failure in AppendContexts, e.g. the options of the comparison. A string matcher only adds them to a failure of the string comparison, also for an item of a collection or a member inside Whose, and not to a failure of another expectation on the same subject. A constraint of your own that compares strings with StringEqualityOptions forwards these contexts from its AppendContexts with options.AppendContexts(contexts), on the options of its evaluation. The ForEvaluation of a StringMatchType also receives the StringMatchSettings, i.e. whether the casing is ignored and the comparer of the caller, and its StringMatcher compares the values after the whitespace options are applied. Core appends these options to the expectation text, e.g. "starts with "Let it" ignoring case". A string match type can also tell Core where its expected value lines up with the subject (Anchors, e.g. a prefix only at the start), count the occurrences of the expected value for a quantified Contains (CountOccurrences of the matcher), and whether a failure lists the differing lines or hints at a different newline style. Through its name, the same option again replaces the earlier match type, and combining it with another comparison throws, e.g. "ByTitle cannot be combined with Equivalent.". Core rejects an unsupported setting of a string match type at the call that specifies the conflict, in either order. The ValidateExpected of a match type is called for every subject, also when nothing is compared with the expected value, e.g. for an empty collection. The items of a collection are compared one after the other with the matcher of the evaluation, so a matcher may keep state across them, e.g. which options matched nothing in any comparison, and report it in AppendContexts. Keep what a single comparison found in its MatchExplanation instead, as a collection compares many items before it explains one. An EquivalencyMatchType<T> compares like IsEquivalentTo. A constraint compares with the matcher that ForEvaluation(new MatchEnvironment(context, cancellationToken)) returns for its evaluation, e.g. with CompareWithExplanation(actual, expected), so that the timeout and the cancellation of the evaluation also end the expectations of an It.Is… in the expected object. It also appends its contexts from this matcher, as only it knows what the comparisons found, e.g. a member to ignore that matched no member.

In the constraint, compare with the options of the evaluation: Compare with the options that ForEvaluation(context, cancellationToken) returns for its evaluation, so that the match type can use the evaluation and keep what its comparisons found. MatchWithExplanation(actual, expected, nameof(expected)) returns a MatchResult, which the constraint keeps for its failure message, as the options keep nothing of a comparison. The string options carry no parameter name: the members that can reject the expected value, e.g. an invalid regex pattern, take the name of the parameter that the ArgumentException reports, e.g. ValidateExpected(expected, nameof(expected)), MatchWithExplanation(…), AreConsideredEqual(actual, expected, nameof(expected)) or CountOccurrences(…). The StringEqualityOptions also write the texts for every match type: GetExpectation(expected, grammars) the expectation and GetExtendedFailure(it, grammars, actual, expected, result) the result, e.g. "it was "Yesterday", which differs …". When the string is a member of the subject, GetExtendedMemberFailure(it, "title", grammars, actual, expected, result) names it like the built-in expectations do, e.g. "it had title "Yesterday", which differs …". For the index options, call MatchesIndex(index, count) on the CollectionIndexOptions for each item, with the number of items or null while it is not known yet. Only true means that the item is at the expected index: null means that a later item could still be, and false that no later item can be, so you can stop there.

An expectation on a property of the subject, e.g. the duration of a track, can return a result that offers the same operators as the built-in property expectations like HasLength(): EqualTo, GreaterThan, Between(…).And(…) and their Not… counterparts, with the same argument checks and texts. Implement the interface for the type of the property: Property type Interface Operators int IIntPropertyResult<TResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations long ILongPropertyResult<TResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations double IDoublePropertyResult<TResult, TToleranceResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations decimal IDecimalPropertyResult<TResult, TToleranceResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations TimeSpan ITimeSpanPropertyResult<TResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations an enum IEnumPropertyResult<TResult, TEnum> EqualTo, NotEqualTo string see String properties The operators are extension methods in the aweXpect namespace. They check the arguments with your Validation, which receives the value and the name of its parameter, e.g. minimum, and pass a PropertyComparison<T> to your Compare method. Compare adds the constraint and returns TResult, the result the caller continues with. Implement the interface explicitly, so that its members do not show up next to the operators: public class DurationResult(IThat<Track?> subject) : ITimeSpanPropertyResult<AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>> { Action<TimeSpan?, string>? ITimeSpanPropertyResult<AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Validation => null; AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> ITimeSpanPropertyResult<AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Compare( PropertyComparison<TimeSpan> comparison) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint(comparison, static (c, it, grammars) => new HasDurationConstraint(it, grammars, c)), subject); } An expectation that returns this result, e.g. HasDuration(), then reads That(track).HasDuration().Between(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)).And(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(4)). In the constraint, comparison.Evaluate(actual) returns the Outcome, and comparison.AppendExpectation(stringBuilder) writes the comparison, e.g. "between" and both values. IsNegated tells that the operator is a negated one, e.g. NotGreaterThan: the outcome already includes the negation, but the text does not, so that you can place the "not" where your sentence needs it, e.g. "has duration not greater than …" or "does not have duration greater than …". The equality operators of a double or decimal property, EqualTo and NotEqualTo, pass a PropertyEqualityComparison<T> to CompareEquality instead, which returns TToleranceResult. The tolerance is set after the operator returned, e.g. .EqualTo(4.5).Within(0.1) or .Within(1).Percent(), so pass comparison.Options to the result you return, e.g. a NumberToleranceResult<TType, TThat, TNumber>, which offers Within. Its text includes the tolerance, e.g. "equal to 4.5 ± 0.1". null and NaN in property comparisons An ordering against null returns Outcome.FailureBothWays. The equality operators of a double or decimal property compare like IsEqualTo(…).Within(…), e.g. NaN is equal to NaN.

The operators of a string property continue with three kinds of results, so they are split over three interfaces, each with its own Validation and Compare method. Implement those whose operators your property offers: Interface Operators Usual TResult IStringEqualityPropertyResult<TResult> EqualTo, NotEqualTo StringEqualityTypeResult<…> IStringAffixPropertyResult<TResult> StartingWith, EndingWith, their negations, NotContaining StringEqualityResult<…> IStringOccurrencePropertyResult<TResult> Containing, with a quantifier such as AtLeast(2) StringOccurrenceCountResult<…> Compare receives a StringPropertyComparison. The string options are set on your result after the operator returned it, e.g. .IgnoringCase(), so pass comparison.Options, and for Containing also comparison.Quantifier, to the result you return, and evaluate the comparison only in your constraint: public class TitleResult(IThat<Track?> subject) : IStringAffixPropertyResult<StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>> { Action<string?, string>? IStringAffixPropertyResult<StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Validation => null; StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IStringAffixPropertyResult<StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Compare( StringPropertyComparison comparison) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint(comparison, static (c, it, grammars) => new HasTitleConstraint(it, grammars, c)), subject, comparison.Options); } An expectation that returns this result, e.g. HasTitle(), then reads That(track).HasTitle().StartingWith("let").IgnoringCase(). In the constraint, call comparison.ValidateExpected() before you look at the subject, so that an unusable expected value, e.g. an invalid regex pattern, throws whichever value the subject has. Then await comparison.Evaluate(actual, context, cancellationToken) compares the value with the options of the evaluation and returns a StringPropertyOutcome, whose Outcome already includes the negation of an operator like NotStartingWith. comparison.AppendExpectation(stringBuilder, grammars) writes the comparison with its options, e.g. "starting with "let" ignoring case", or "starts with …" with ExpectationGrammars.Active, and outcome.AppendResult(stringBuilder, "title", grammars, indentation) writes the result, e.g. "title was "Yesterday", which differs at index 0: …". Like for the other property types, neither text includes the negation of the operator, so that you can place it where your sentence needs it: for a comparison that IsNegated, add ExpectationGrammars.Negated to the grammars, e.g. grammars.Negate(), which writes "not starting with …" or "does not start with …". outcome.AppendContexts(contexts) adds the contexts of the options. A null string property A null value fails a comparison that looks into the value, e.g. a prefix or an occurrence, both ways.

An operator of your own for any of these property types, except string, passes the comparison that PropertyComparison<T>.Satisfying(predicate, expectation) creates to Compare, like the built-in operators do. It works on every result that implements the interface, also on those of aweXpect.Core and of other packages. For example, the day of the week on which an album was released can be on a weekend: public static TResult OnWeekend<TResult>(this IEnumPropertyResult<TResult, DayOfWeek> result) => result.Compare(PropertyComparison<DayOfWeek>.Satisfying( static day => day is DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday, "on a weekend")); public static TResult NotOnWeekend<TResult>(this IEnumPropertyResult<TResult, DayOfWeek> result) => result.Compare(PropertyComparison<DayOfWeek>.Satisfying( static day => day is DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday, "on a weekend", isNegated: true)); The predicate receives the value of the property, which is null when the property is. The expectation is the text of the comparison without its negation and follows the name of the property, e.g. "has release day on a weekend" or "whose release day is on a weekend". For a negated operator pass isNegated: true with the same predicate and text: the comparison is then met when the predicate does not hold, and the result places the "not", e.g. "does not have release day on a weekend" or "whose release day is not on a weekend". Create a comparison that does not depend on an argument once and reuse it, as it is immutable.

A constraint decides whether the subject meets the expectation, and its result writes the failure message. This page shows the kinds of constraints and results, and the rules they follow for negation, null subjects and side effects. Namespaces used on this page using System.Text; using System.Threading; using System.Threading.Tasks; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Core.Constraints; using aweXpect.Core.EvaluationContext; using aweXpect.Formatting; using aweXpect.Results; using static aweXpect.Formatting.Format;

The basis for expectations are constraints. You can add different constraints to the ExpectationBuilder that is available for the IThat<T>. They differ in the input and output parameters for the IsMetBy method: Constraint IsMetBy receives Use it IValueConstraint<T> the actual value for a synchronous check IAsyncConstraint<T> the actual value and a CancellationToken for asynchronous work or to observe the timeout IContextConstraint<T>, IAsyncContextConstraint<T> additionally an IEvaluationContext to share data, to read a collection once or for side effects IsMetBy returns a ConstraintResult, which decides the outcome and writes the expectation and the result texts of the failure message. The evaluation context The IEvaluationContext allows storing and receiving data between expectations. This mechanism is used for example to avoid enumerating an IEnumerable multiple times across multiple constraints. A value stored while an item of a collection or a member after Whose or Which is evaluated is only received by the expectations on that item or member, so a value cached for one item is not handed to the next one. Its Cancellation describes the cancellation of the evaluation: the Token (the same token that an asynchronous constraint receives), the effective Timeout, and the Reason of a cancellation: None, the Timeout, or the Caller. With OnCompleted, a constraint registers a callback that runs when the whole expectation is decided, see side effects.

An IAsyncConstraint<T> receives the CancellationToken of the expectation, which is canceled when the timeout (WithTimeout) elapses or the caller cancels (WithCancellation). Pass it on to the asynchronous work: public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(Track? actual, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { Actual = actual; if (actual is not null) { Outcome = await IsInCatalogAsync(actual, cancellationToken) ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } An OperationCanceledException from that token needs no handling: a timeout fails the expectation with "did not finish within …", and a cancellation by the caller leaves it inconclusive. Stopping without an exception A constraint that stops at the cancellation without throwing leaves its Outcome undecided. A timeout then fails the expectation in the same way. After a cancellation, the helper classes write the result text with AppendUndecidedResult, which you can override. By default it writes "it could not be verified, because the evaluation was already canceled". Leave the Outcome undecided only for a cancellation. An expectation whose outcome stays undecided although nothing was canceled, e.g. because one branch of IsMetBy does not set it or a collection constraint does not call Complete(), fails with "it could not be verified, because the expectation did not decide its outcome". A timeout of your own An expectation that waits for something outside aweXpect with a timeout of its own, e.g. Within(timeout), cancels its wait with CancelAfter of the IEvaluationContext and measures it with GetTimestamp() and GetElapsedTime(…). They all use the clock of the evaluation, which is the real one unless the caller sets another with WithTimeProvider(…), so that the timeout and the measured time agree, also on a virtual clock: using CancellationTokenSource waitCts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(cancellationToken); context.CancelAfter(waitCts, timeout); long startTimestamp = context.GetTimestamp(); try { await WaitForTrackAsync(actual, waitCts.Token); Outcome = Outcome.Success; } catch (OperationCanceledException) { Outcome = context.Cancellation.HasWaitElapsed(timeout, context.GetElapsedTime(startTimestamp)) ? Outcome.Failure : Outcome.Undecided; } HasWaitElapsed tells a wait that reached its timeout, which fails the expectation, apart from a cancellation by the caller or a shorter timeout of the evaluation, which leave it undecided.

All constraints should also provide the expectations and results for the negated case, so that they are compatible with DoesNotComplyWith. The recommended practice is to use the same class for the constraint and its ConstraintResult, derived from one of the following helper classes: Helper class null subject Use it when the expectation ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<T> fails the expectation and its negation inspects the subject ConstraintResult.WithEqualToValue<T> is an ordinary value, compared with the expected compares for equality or identity ConstraintResult.WithValue<T> is not handled handles null itself or has a non-nullable subject All three take the name of the subject (it) and the grammars in their constructor and expose the name as the inherited It property. You set the Actual property in the IsMetBy method and override AppendNormalExpectation, AppendNegatedExpectation and AppendNormalResult. By default, the negated result is described like the normal one; override AppendNegatedResult when it differs, e.g. "it was" for a negated "it was not". WithEqualToValue<T> additionally takes a flag indicating if the expected value is null. The IsRadioFriendlyConstraint of your first expectation derives from ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Track>, as it inspects the subject. The helper classes let .And combine the result texts like the built-in expectations, e.g. "it was 2 and was not even" instead of "it was 2 and it was not even". Pass it to the base class and use the inherited It property. Deriving from ConstraintResult directly A constraint can also derive from ConstraintResult directly. It then writes the texts in AppendExpectation and AppendResult, returns the value in TryGetStoredValue and implements NegateInPlace() itself. This example does not support the negated case: private sealed class IsRadioFriendlyConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars) : ConstraintResult(grammars), IValueConstraint<Track?> { private Track? _actual; public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(Track? actual) { _actual = actual; Outcome = actual?.Duration <= TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3) ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; return this; } public override void AppendExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is radio friendly"); public override void AppendResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { stringBuilder.Append(it).Append(" was "); Formatter.Format(stringBuilder, _actual?.Duration); stringBuilder.Append(" long"); } public override bool TryGetStoredValue<TValue>(out TValue? value) where TValue : default { if (_actual is TValue typedValue) { value = typedValue; return true; } value = default; return typeof(TValue).IsAssignableFrom(typeof(Track)); } protected override void NegateInPlace() => throw Tracing.WriteException( new NotSupportedException("Negation of IsRadioFriendly is not supported.")); } NegateInPlace() is called whenever the expectation is negated, e.g. by DoesNotComplyWith(x => x.IsRadioFriendly()), and negates the result itself. Doing nothing would silently check the non-negated expectation instead, so a constraint that cannot be negated throws, like the built-in ExecutesIn(). To combine the result texts with .And like the helper classes, override LeadingSubject and TrailingSubject with GetSubjectOfResult(it).

A constraint that supports the negated case also allows you to write an explicit negated expectation with the .Invert() method: /// <summary> /// Verifies that the <paramref name="subject"/> is not radio friendly. /// </summary> public static AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsNotRadioFriendly( this IThat<Track?> subject) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new IsRadioFriendlyConstraint(it, grammars).Invert()), subject); .InvertIf(isNegated) negates the constraint only when isNegated is true, so that an expectation and its negation can share one implementation.

Which of the three helper classes to pick is decided by how your expectation treats a null subject, and that follows the rule that all built-in expectations follow (see null subjects): A null subject fails an expectation and its negation, unless the expectation is about null: equality and identity comparisons, where null is a legitimate value on either side, or an explicit null or tri-state check. Your expectation inspects the subject, e.g. its length, its type or its items: use ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<T>. IsNotEmpty() fails for a null subject just like IsEmpty() does. This includes expectations that take a value but do not compare for equality, e.g. HasValue(2), IsGreaterThan or IsNotBetween. Your expectation compares the subject for equality or identity against a value the caller supplied: use ConstraintResult.WithEqualToValue<T> and pass whether the expected value is null. IsEqualTo(null) succeeds for a null subject, IsNotEqualTo(null) fails and IsNotEqualTo("Yesterday") succeeds. Your subject cannot be null, or your expectation decides every null case itself, e.g. IsNull() or IsOneOf(...), whose expected values may or may not include null: use ConstraintResult.WithValue<T>. WithValue<T> applies no null policy of its own: a failure that you set for a null subject in IsMetBy is inverted into a success when the expectation is negated. Set Outcome.FailureBothWays instead.

After an expectation that fails for a null subject, the subject can't be null any more. Mark such an expectation with the [GuaranteesNotNull] attribute from aweXpect.Core, so that the nullability suppressor of the aweXpect package suppresses the nullability warnings for the subject after your expectation, as it does after IsNotNull(): [GuaranteesNotNull] public static AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsRadioFriendly(this IThat<Track?> subject) => // ... Track[] tracks = [new("Love Me Do", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 22)), new("Hey Jude", new TimeSpan(0, 7, 11))]; Track? track = tracks.FirstOrDefault(t => t.Title == "Love Me Do"); await That(track).IsRadioFriendly(); string title = track.Title; // no CS8602 Only mark an expectation that fails for a null subject regardless of its other arguments, e.g. one that uses ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<T>. A wrongly marked expectation hides real nullability warnings. The expectation has to be an extension method on IThat<TSubject>. Expectations combined with And An expectation of your package before .And, as in That(track).IsRadioFriendly().And.IsNotNull(), keeps the subject for the suppressor only when it returns an aweXpect result for the same IThat<TSubject>, such as AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>. An expectation that returns an IThat<…> itself could continue with a different subject, so the suppressor ignores the expectations after it.

Check the arguments in the extension method itself, so that a wrong argument fails right where the caller passes it. Use the wording of the built-in expectations: a missing argument reads "The 'title' cannot be null.", and any other invalid argument is described in a complete sentence, as the message conventions explain. Throw the exception via Tracing.WriteException, which also hands it to the trace writer that users enable with Customize.aweXpect.EnableTracing(…). Core has no public helper for this, so add a small one to your extension: internal static void ThrowIfNull(object? value, string paramName) { if (value is null) { string message = $"The '{paramName}' cannot be null."; throw Tracing.WriteException(new ArgumentNullException(paramName, message)); } } public static AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> HasTitle(this IThat<Track?> subject, string title) { ThrowIfNull(title, nameof(title)); // ... }

The first type argument of the result, e.g. Track in AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>, is the type of the value that the expectation passes on. Awaiting the expectation returns this value, and an AndOrWhoseResult<TType, TThat> also continues with Whose on a member of it: public static AndOrWhoseResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsRadioFriendly(this IThat<Track?> subject) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new IsRadioFriendlyConstraint(it, grammars)), subject); Track track = new("Love Me Do", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 22)); Track verifiedTrack = await That(track).IsRadioFriendly(); await That(track).IsRadioFriendly().Whose(t => t.Title, title => title.StartsWith("Love")); Both ask the TryGetStoredValue<TValue> method of the ConstraintResult for the value, so a constraint that narrows or converts the subject returns the converted value there. The helper classes return their Actual value. How the stored value is used Whose and AndWhose access the member on that value when the expectation is met; when it is not met, a member of a converted value is not evaluated, only its expectations are shown. A stored null value of a matching type still returns true, so that awaiting the expectation returns null. When TryGetStoredValue returns false for the type, awaiting the successful expectation returns the default of the type, e.g. after an .Or whose earlier alternative was met. TryGetValue<TValue> builds on it and only returns true for a value that is not null. A result of your own that derives from AndOrResult<TType, TThat> reaches the ExpectationBuilder through the protected property of the same name, e.g. to continue with ExpectationBuilder.And() or ExpectationBuilder.Or(). For the options a result offers, see options.

When a constraint calls code of the caller while it is evaluated, e.g. a predicate, a member selector or a comparer, call it through UserCode.Invoke. An exception it throws then fails the expectation and its negation alike, with the exception as inner exception, instead of aborting the evaluation: Outcome = UserCode.Invoke(predicate, actual, "the predicate") ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; The optional last argument names the code in the failure message, e.g. "the predicate did throw an InvalidOperationException"; without it, the subject is named ("it did throw …"). For an asynchronous predicate, use UserCode.InvokeAsync(() => predicate(actual), "the predicate", cancellationToken), which throws an OperationCanceledException unchanged while the cancellationToken is canceled. An exception that your constraint throws itself, e.g. to reject an invalid argument, is still thrown as it is.

Some expectations cannot be answered at all, e.g. because the subject is null, the values are not comparable or code of the caller threw. Negating such an expectation does not make it true, so it fails the expectation and its negation alike. Set Outcome.FailureBothWays in IsMetBy to say so: catch (Exception exception) { _exception = exception; Outcome = Outcome.FailureBothWays; } Outcome.FailureBothWays fails the expectation like Outcome.Failure, but a negation keeps it. WithNotNullValue<T> reports it for a null subject. When you derive from ConstraintResult directly, swap only Success and Failure in your NegateInPlace() and keep FailureBothWays. Reading an outcome Code that reads an outcome treats Outcome.Failure and Outcome.FailureBothWays alike as a failed expectation. An expectation that evaluates nested expectations, e.g. on the items of a collection, checks for Outcome.FailureBothWays to find out whether an item was answered.

A constraint that changes something outside the evaluation, e.g. writes a file, must not do so in IsMetBy: at that point it cannot know whether it is negated, e.g. by DoesNotComplyWith, or whether another branch of an Or decides the expectation. Register a callback with IEvaluationContext.OnCompleted instead. It runs after the whole expectation is decided and every negation is applied, before a failure is thrown: public interface ITrackArchive { bool Contains(Track track); Task AddAsync(Track track, CancellationToken cancellationToken); } private sealed class IsArchivedConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, ITrackArchive archive) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Track>(it, grammars), IContextConstraint<Track?> { public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(Track? actual, IEvaluationContext context) { Actual = actual; Outcome = actual is not null && archive.Contains(actual) ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; context.OnCompleted(ArchiveAsync); return this; } private async ValueTask ArchiveAsync(CompletedEvaluation evaluation, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { if (evaluation.Outcome == Outcome.Failure && Outcome == Outcome.Failure && !IsNegated && Actual is not null) { await archive.AddAsync(Actual, cancellationToken); } } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is archived"); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" was not"); protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is not archived"); protected override void AppendNegatedResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" was"); } The CompletedEvaluation has the Outcome of the whole expectation: Success, Failure (also after a timeout) or Undecided, when the evaluation was canceled. The constraint itself knows its own Outcome, which already includes the negation, and whether it IsNegated. Each delegate runs once, even when the constraint is evaluated several times, e.g. for each item of a collection or each check of Eventually() or Within(…), so register a method of the constraint, as above. Its state is then the one of the last evaluation. Negation in a constraint of your own, order and cancellation of the callbacks A constraint that derives from ConstraintResult directly tracks its negation by overriding NegateInPlace(), which is called for every negation that applies to it, also within .And, .Or, Whose and Which: protected override void NegateInPlace() { _isNegated = !_isNegated; Outcome = Outcome switch { Outcome.Success => Outcome.Failure, Outcome.Failure => Outcome.Success, _ => Outcome, }; } The callbacks run in the order in which they were registered first. An exception they throw is thrown by the expectation. They receive the cancellation token of the caller, which a timeout of the expectation does not cancel. A quantifier, e.g. in All().ComplyWith(…), counts the items that meet the item expectations without negating them, so a constraint on the items is never negated, not even in DoesNotComplyWith(c => c.All().ComplyWith(…)) or for None(). Decide on the Outcome of the whole expectation there.

The factory passed to AddConstraint usually captures the arguments of the expectation, which allocates a closure and a delegate for every expectation. To avoid that, pass the arguments as state to a static lambda: public static AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsShorterThan(this IThat<Track?> subject, TimeSpan maximum) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint(maximum, static (max, it, grammars) => new IsShorterThanConstraint(it, grammars, max)), subject); For several arguments, pass a tuple as the state.

You can add your own customizations on top of the AwexpectCustomization class by adding extension methods. Namespaces used on this page using System.Reflection; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Core.Extending; using aweXpect.Customization;

You can add a simple customizable value (e.g. an int): public static class PlaylistCustomizationExtensions { public static ICustomizationValueSetter<int> MaximumPlaylistLength( this AwexpectCustomization awexpectCustomization) => new CustomizationValue<int>(awexpectCustomization, "MusicStore.MaximumPlaylistLength", 100); } CustomizationValue<TValue> from aweXpect.Customization stores the value under the key. The key identifies the value, so choose one that no other package uses, e.g. prefixed with the name of your package. A null that was set is returned as null, not as the default value, so pass a validate callback that rejects null if your value must not be null, as the group below does. This allows expectations to access the value: // will return the default value of 100 int maximumPlaylistLength = Customize.aweXpect.MaximumPlaylistLength().Get(); And users can customize the value: using (Customize.aweXpect.MaximumPlaylistLength().Set(50)) { // will now return 50 int maximumPlaylistLength = Customize.aweXpect.MaximumPlaylistLength().Get(); } // will now return again the default value of 100, because the customization lifetime was disposed _ = Customize.aweXpect.MaximumPlaylistLength().Get(); You can also use this mechanism for complex objects like classes, but then they can only be changed as a whole and not property by property.

For a list, use CustomizationListValue<TItem> instead of a CustomizationValue<IReadOnlyList<TItem>>: public static class TrackTitleCustomizationExtensions { public static ICustomizationValueSetter<IReadOnlyList<string>> IgnoredTrackTitles( this AwexpectCustomization awexpectCustomization) => new CustomizationListValue<string>(awexpectCustomization, "MusicStore.IgnoredTrackTitles", Array.AsReadOnly<string>(["Intro", "Outro"])); } Set stores a read-only copy of the list and rejects null. Otherwise a caller who keeps the list they set, or who casts the returned list to a mutable one, could change the value outside its scope. The default value is returned as it is, so pass a read-only list. A validate callback receives the copy, e.g. to reject null items.

To offer several related values, add a group: a class that exposes one ICustomizationValueSetter<TValue> per value. Each value is stored under its own key, so it can be set and restored independently of the other values of the group: public static class MusicStoreCustomizationExtensions { public static MusicStoreCustomization MusicStore(this AwexpectCustomization awexpectCustomization) => new(awexpectCustomization); public class MusicStoreCustomization { internal MusicStoreCustomization(IAwexpectCustomization awexpectCustomization) { MaximumRadioDuration = new CustomizationValue<TimeSpan>( awexpectCustomization, "MusicStore.MaximumRadioDuration", TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3)); DefaultGenre = new CustomizationValue<string>( awexpectCustomization, "MusicStore.DefaultGenre", "Rock", value => { if (value is null) { throw Tracing.WriteException( new ArgumentNullException(nameof(value), "The 'value' cannot be null.")); } }); } public ICustomizationValueSetter<TimeSpan> MaximumRadioDuration { get; } public ICustomizationValueSetter<string> DefaultGenre { get; } } } The validate callback checks a value before Set stores it, so that Set(null) throws and changes nothing. Expectations access each value on its own: // will return the default value of 3 minutes TimeSpan maximumRadioDuration = Customize.aweXpect.MusicStore().MaximumRadioDuration.Get(); And users customize each value on its own: using (Customize.aweXpect.MusicStore().DefaultGenre.Set("Pop")) { // will use "Pop" as the default genre // but keep any configured maximum radio duration } Both kinds of customizations work with global defaults without any change: Customize.aweXpect.Global.MaximumPlaylistLength().Set(50) or Customize.aweXpect.Global.MusicStore().DefaultGenre.Set(…) stores the value for all async flows, because Global is an AwexpectCustomization as well. Their lifetimes behave like the ones of the built-in values, also when they are disposed out of order.

The built-in groups Equivalency(), Formatting() and Settings() implement IAwexpectCustomization as well, so you can add a value to one of them with an extension method on the group: public static class TrackFormattingCustomizationExtensions { public static ICustomizationValueSetter<string> TrackDurationFormat( this AwexpectCustomization.FormattingCustomization formatting) => new CustomizationValue<string>(formatting, "MusicStore.Formatting.TrackDurationFormat", @"m\:ss"); } Users then find the value next to the built-in ones, e.g. Customize.aweXpect.Formatting().TrackDurationFormat(). A group stores its values in the customization it was taken from, so Customize.aweXpect.Global.Formatting().TrackDurationFormat().Set(…) stores the value for all async flows.

If your extension scans assemblies, skip the ones that the user excluded with ExcludedAssemblyPrefixes. AssemblyPrefixes.IsExcluded from aweXpect.Core.Extending matches an assembly name with the same rule as aweXpect, at a segment boundary of the name: public static class CatalogAssemblyScanner { public static IEnumerable<Assembly> ScannedAssemblies() { IReadOnlyList<string> prefixes = Customize.aweXpect.Settings().ExcludedAssemblyPrefixes.Get(); return AppDomain.CurrentDomain.GetAssemblies() .Where(assembly => !AssemblyPrefixes.IsExcluded(assembly.GetName().Name, prefixes)); } } The overload without prefixes, e.g. AssemblyPrefixes.IsExcluded("System.Text"), reads the current setting on each call, so read the prefixes once when you check many names.

A failure message shows values the same way in every expectation. Format the values of your extension like the built-in ones, and teach aweXpect how to format the types that your extension declares. Namespaces used on this page using System.Text; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Equivalency; using aweXpect.Formatting; using static aweXpect.Formatting.Format;

Format every value with Formatter.Format from aweXpect.Formatting.Format, so that it looks the same as in the built-in messages and respects the formatting settings: Value Formatted as null <null> string "Let It Be", in quotes and truncated after MaximumStringLength characters char 'a' numbers 42 or -3.5, independent of the current culture TimeSpan 0:02 or 0:00.015 DateTime 2024-12-24T13:15:00.0000000 Type its C# name without namespace, e.g. int or List<string> enum Read, or Read | Write for a combination of flags Exception its type and message, e.g. InvalidOperationException: Yesterday collection ["Help!", "Revolver"], with (… and 2 more) after MaximumNumberOfCollectionItems items other objects their ToString() if it is overridden, otherwise their public members, e.g. Album { Title = "Abbey Road" } The FormattingOptions change the layout: FormattingOptions.MultipleLines puts every item of a collection on its own line, e.g. for a context, FormattingOptions.WithType prefixes the type (int[] [1, 2]), and FormattingOptions.Indented(indentation) indents the following lines. Without options, an object that is not an item of a collection puts each member on its own line; FormattingOptions.SingleLine keeps it on one line as in the table. FormattingOptions.Snapshot, or IsSnapshot = true on any other options, writes the value for a snapshot: without shortening it, and the items of collections whose order depends on hash codes or threads, like a HashSet<T> or a ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>, sorted by their formatted text or key, so that it is the same in every run. Register an IValueFormatter to format your own types, see value formatters. FormatValue on the FormattingOptions decides for every nested value whether it is written (ValueFormatting.Write), left out (ValueFormatting.Omit) or replaced by another value that is formatted in its place (ValueFormatting.Replace(value)), e.g. to leave out values that change from run to run in a snapshot. It is offered the members of objects that are written member-wise, the items of tuples and collections, and the values of dictionary entries, as a FormattedValue with its Kind, Name, Type, DeclaringType and Path. The path has the format of an equivalency comparison (Artist.Name, Tracks[0].Id, Ratings[4.5], Seats[0,1]), with [*] as the index of an item of a collection whose order depends on hash codes or threads, like a HashSet<T>, so that the rules to ignore members in an equivalency comparison can be reused: MemberToIgnore ignoreDuration = new MemberToIgnore.ByName("Duration"); FormattingOptions options = FormattingOptions.Indented("") with { IsSnapshot = true, FormatValue = value => ignoreDuration.IgnoreMember(value.Path, value.Type) ? ValueFormatting.Omit : value.Name == "Title" ? ValueFormatting.Replace("{title}") : ValueFormatting.Write, }; string snapshot = Formatter.Format(new Track("Let It Be", TimeSpan.FromSeconds(243)), options); Exceptions in snapshots, FormatValue, escaping and limits A snapshot writes an exception member-wise, e.g. ArgumentException { Message = "…", ParamName = "track" }, with its message, its own public members, its Data when it is not empty and its inner exceptions (all of them for an AggregateException), but without StackTrace, TargetSite, Source, HelpLink and HResult, which change between builds, runtimes and Native AOT. FormatValue is not offered the value itself, nor the keys of a dictionary, nor anything inside a value that a registered IValueFormatter or its own ToString() renders. A member is only read when it is written or when GetValue() asks for it, so a member that is left out is not read at all. Leaving out an item of a tuple shifts the following items, so that their position in the parentheses no longer matches their position in the tuple. A getter that throws is written as the usual placeholder, while an exception of FormatValue itself is thrown out of the formatting. Without FormatValue, nothing changes. Chars and strings are always written on a single line and escaped like C# literals, so that every character can be told apart: a backslash, the enclosing quote, line breaks, tabs, control characters, invisible characters (like a non-breaking or a zero-width space), combining marks in text that is not normalized (like the accent of a decomposed é) and unpaired surrogates are shown as \\, \" (or \' in a char), \n, \r, \t, \0 or \uXXXX. Exception messages and the ToString() of other objects are not quoted, so only their line breaks, control and invisible characters are escaped when they are written on a single line. A multi-dimensional array is written with a nested collection per dimension, e.g. [[1, 2], [3, 4]] for an int[2,2]. Nested objects, collections and tuples are written up to 20 levels deep and up to 1000 of them per value. Beyond that, their content is left out as { … }, [ … ] or ( … ), so that a long chain or a graph that shares its nodes on every level neither overflows the stack nor grows without bound. An object or collection that contains itself is written as { *recursive* } or [ *recursive* ] where it repeats. Snapshot options lift these limits and those of the formatting settings; a value that is nested too deeply for the remaining stack then throws an InsufficientExecutionStackException instead.

A value formatter returns false for every value it does not format, so that the next formatter or the built-in formatting applies. This TrackFormatter writes a Track with its title and duration: internal sealed class TrackFormatter : IValueFormatter { public bool TryFormat(StringBuilder stringBuilder, object value, FormattingOptions? options) { if (value is not Track track) { return false; } stringBuilder.Append(track.Title).Append(" ("); Format.Formatter.Format(stringBuilder, track.Duration); stringBuilder.Append(')'); return true; } } Register it with ValueFormatter.Register(new TrackFormatter()) in a module initializer, which runs before your extension is first used. A registered formatter applies process-wide, to all threads and async flows, until the returned IDisposable is disposed. It is asked for every value that is not null, including built-in types such as DateTime or int, whether the value is formatted on its own, as an item of a collection or as a member of an object. When several registered formatters can format a value, the most recently registered one is used. Register a formatter only for the types that your extension declares. The module initializer runs before any of them is used, so their messages never depend on the order of the tests. A formatter for a type that your extension does not own, e.g. System.Version, would only apply to the tests that run after the first test that used your extension, and would change how other tests format it. Add such a formatter to your expectations instead.

ExpectationBuilder.AddFormatter formats the values of one expectation with a formatter, before the registered ones. It applies while the expectation is evaluated and while its failure message is created, also to the expectations chained to it, e.g. collection expectations on the items of a member, but never outside of the expectation: internal static class MusicStoreFormatting { private static readonly IValueFormatter VersionFormatter = new ShortVersionFormatter(); internal static ExpectationBuilder WithVersionFormatter(this ExpectationBuilder expectationBuilder) => expectationBuilder.AddFormatter(VersionFormatter); private sealed class ShortVersionFormatter : IValueFormatter { public bool TryFormat(StringBuilder stringBuilder, object value, FormattingOptions? options) { if (value is not Version version) { return false; } stringBuilder.Append('v').Append(version.ToString(3)); return true; } } } When the expectation is nested in another one, e.g. with ComplyWith, or combined with others in Expect.ThatAll or Expect.ThatAny, the whole failure message uses the formatter. Pass a cached instance, as adding the same formatter again has no effect.

An expectation that only checks a condition on its subject doesn't need a constraint class of its own: mark a static method that decides the condition with [GenerateExpectation] from aweXpect.Core.Extending, and the source generator in the aweXpect.Core package writes the extension methods, the constraint and its failure messages. It runs in every project that references aweXpect.Core, directly or through aweXpect, so an extension package can use it as well as a test project. Namespaces used on this page using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Core.Extending; public static partial class ThatTrack { [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}LongerThan", "is {not} longer than {minimum}")] private static bool IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration > minimum; } Track track = new("Love Me Do", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 22)); await That(track).IsLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)); await That(track).IsNotLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3));

The method is static and returns bool, Task<bool> or ValueTask<bool>, or a PredicateResult instead of the bool when it cannot always answer. Its first parameter is the subject, the other parameters become the parameters of the expectation. A CancellationToken parameter marked with [EvaluationCancellationToken] receives the token of the evaluation and is no parameter of the expectation. It can be at any position after the subject, e.g. before a params parameter. A CancellationToken parameter that is not marked is a parameter of the expectation like any other. [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}OneOf", "is {not} one of {titles}")] private static async Task<bool> IsOneOf(Track track, [EvaluationCancellationToken] CancellationToken cancellationToken, params string[] titles) => titles.Contains(await LookUpTitle(track, cancellationToken)); It is declared in a top-level, non-generic, static partial class that is not file-local, which receives the generated extension methods. The method itself can be private. Accessibility of the generated methods The generated extension methods are public, unless the class, the subject or a parameter type is internal: then they are internal as well.

The name is the name of the expectation. A {Not} in it, or a NegatedName, also generates the negated expectation, e.g. "Is{Not}LongerThan" generates IsLongerThan and IsNotLongerThan. The expectationText follows the message conventions. {not} is removed from the expectation and becomes "not" in its negation. Any other placeholder, e.g. {minimum}, names a parameter, whose formatted value replaces it. When "Not" and "not" in place of {Not} and {not} don't read well, give the negated name in NegatedName and the negated text in NegatedExpectationText, with the same placeholders. Every expectation can be negated with DoesNotComplyWith, even one without a negated name, so the text needs either {not} or a NegatedExpectationText: [GenerateExpectation("HasTitle", "has title {title}", NegatedName = "DoesNotHaveTitle", NegatedExpectationText = "does not have title {title}")] private static bool HasTitle(Track track, string title) => track.Title == title; The negated expectation names its parameters like the method. To give a parameter another name there, e.g. unexpected instead of expected, mark it with [NegatedParameterName]. The name applies to the signature, the argument check and the derived XML documentation of the negated expectation, while the placeholders of both texts keep the name of the method's parameter: [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}Named", "is {not} named {expected}")] private static bool IsNamed(Track track, [NegatedParameterName("unexpected")] string expected) => track.Title == expected; This generates IsNamed(string expected) and IsNotNamed(string unexpected). The result after "but" shows the formatted subject. To describe it differently, name a static method that returns the text after the subject in Result. It takes the subject, optionally followed by the other parameters: [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}LongerThan", "is {not} longer than {minimum}", Result = nameof(DescribeDuration))] private static bool IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration > minimum; private static string DescribeDuration(Track track) => $"was {track.Duration:m\\:ss} long"; Failure message Expected that track is longer than 3:00, but it was 2:22 long To describe the subject itself, the method can end with a string and an ExpectationGrammars parameter. It then receives how the subject is referred to, e.g. "it", and returns the whole text after "but": private static string DescribeDuration(Track track, string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars) => $"{it}{grammars.SubjectVerb(it, " was ", " were ")}{track.Duration:m\\:ss} long"; The XML documentation is derived from the expectation text. Summary, NegatedSummary, Remarks and NegatedRemarks replace or extend it with XML documentation of your own.

The generated expectations follow the rule for null subjects, and the type of the subject parameter decides how: Subject parameter Generated expectations a reference type, e.g. Track on IThat<Track?>; null fails the expectation and its negation a value type, e.g. TimeSpan on IThat<TimeSpan> and on IThat<TimeSpan?>, where null fails both a nullable type, e.g. Track? or TimeSpan? on IThat<Track?> or IThat<TimeSpan?>; the method decides about null a nullable type with [DisallowNull] on the nullable type; null fails the expectation and its negation Set NullableOverload = false to generate no overload on the nullable value type, e.g. when a separate class of yours already holds the expectations on it. An expectation that fails for a null subject is marked with [GuaranteesNotNull]. When the method decides about null, [NotNullWhen] on its subject parameter tells which of the two expectations guarantees a subject that is not null, like on string.IsNullOrEmpty: [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}Untitled", "is {not} untitled")] private static bool IsUntitled([NotNullWhen(false)] Track? track) => track is null || track.Title.Length == 0; Here IsNotUntitled() fails for a null subject, so the subject cannot be null after it.

When the method cannot decide for some subjects, e.g. a track without a duration, it returns a PredicateResult. A bool converts implicitly, so only that case needs PredicateResult.FailureBothWays with the reason, which follows "it" in the failure message: [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}LongerThan", "is {not} longer than {minimum}")] private static PredicateResult IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration <= TimeSpan.Zero ? PredicateResult.FailureBothWays("had no duration") : track.Duration > minimum; Failure message Expected that track is not longer than 3:00, but it had no duration The expectation and its negation fail alike, as negating a question that cannot be answered does not make it true. The Result method still describes a subject that the method decided about.

[GenerateCollectionExpectation] generates an expectation on the items of a collection from the same kind of method, e.g. AreLongerThan for That(tracks).All().AreLongerThan(…). It takes the name, the expectation text on a single item and its plural: [GenerateCollectionExpectation("AreLongerThan", "is longer than {minimum}", "are longer than {minimum}")] private static bool IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration > minimum; Together with [GenerateExpectation], the text on a single item can be left out, as it is the expectation text of [GenerateExpectation] without {not}: [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}LongerThan", "is {not} longer than {minimum}")] [GenerateCollectionExpectation("AreLongerThan", "are longer than {minimum}")] private static bool IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration > minimum; await That(tracks).All().AreLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)); await That(tracks).AtLeast(2).AreLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)); await That(tracks).None().AreLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); The method follows the rules above, and its first parameter is the item. The expectation text describes a single item, e.g. "is longer than … for all items". The plural text is used where the quantifier is the subject, e.g. "has values of which at least 2 are longer than …". The quantifier carries the negation. The result counts the items, e.g. "but only 1 of 3 were", with "did" instead of "were" when the text does not start with a form of "be". The failure message lists the matching or not matching items and the collection. A null item does not match, unless the item parameter is nullable: then the method decides. [DisallowNull] and NullableOverload work like for a subject. NullItemFailsBothWays = true makes a null item fail the expectation and its negation instead, like a null subject, e.g. but for the item at index 1, it was <null>. Use it when the question cannot be answered for a null item, instead of a nullable item parameter that returns PredicateResult.FailureBothWays for it. An item that the method cannot answer fails the expectation and its negation, e.g. "but for the item at index 1, it had no duration", unless the items before already determine the outcome. Summary and Remarks replace or extend the XML documentation, which is derived from the plural text. Which collections and item types are extended The expectation extends the items of every kind of collection that can hold the item: an IEnumerable<T>, an ImmutableArray<T> and, on .NET 8 or later, an IAsyncEnumerable<T>. The items of a reference type are extended as nullable, so that the expectation applies to a List<Track>, a List<Track?> and a collection of a type derived from Track. The type of the item can be the only type parameter of the method, when a constraint restricts it to reference types and no other parameter uses it, e.g. IsLive<TRecording>(TRecording recording) where TRecording : Recording. The expectations are then generic as well and keep the type of the items, e.g. for a collection of albums.

CollectionOverload = true also generates the expectation as an overload directly on the collection, which all items have to meet, and a NegatedName generates an expectation directly on the collection, which no item may meet. The two are independent: CollectionOverload only adds the positive overload, so the negated one on the collection needs a NegatedName, while the quantified None() is always available. [GenerateCollectionExpectation("AreLongerThan", "is longer than {minimum}", "are longer than {minimum}", CollectionOverload = true, NegatedName = "AreNotLongerThan")] private static bool IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration > minimum; await That(tracks).AreLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)); await That(tracks).AreNotLongerThan(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); The quantifier is the subject of the text, e.g. "all are longer than …" and "none are longer than …", whose negations read "not all are longer than …" and "at least one is longer than …". The result counts the items like above, e.g. "but only 2 of 3 were". The collection is read to its end, so that the failure message lists every item that does not meet the expectation, or that meets it for the NegatedName. Use a quantifier like All() instead on a collection that never ends. Extended collections, XML documentation and parameter names They extend an IEnumerable<T> and, on .NET 8 or later, an IAsyncEnumerable<T> of the item, and a null collection fails them and their negations. The summary of the XML documentation is derived from the plural text, e.g. "Verifies that all items are longer than …" and "Verifies that no items are longer than …"; the Remarks apply to them as well. A parameter marked with [NegatedParameterName] has that name in the NegatedName expectation, also in a <paramref> of the Remarks, and keeps its name in all other expectations.

A StringEqualityOptions parameter marked with [ExpectationOptions] gives the expectation the string options, e.g. AsPrefix(), IgnoringCase() or AsRegex(), which compare with the string parameter of the method: [GenerateCollectionExpectation("HaveTitle", "has title {expected}", "have title {expected}", CollectionOverload = true, NegatedName = "DoNotHaveTitle")] private static ValueTask<bool> HasTitle(Track track, [NegatedParameterName("unexpected")] string expected, [ExpectationOptions] StringEqualityOptions options) => options.AreConsideredEqual(track.Title, expected, nameof(expected)); await That(tracks).HaveTitle("Intro").AsPrefix().IgnoringCase(); await That(tracks).AtLeast(2).HaveTitle("*live*").AsWildcard(); The options are not a parameter of the expectation: every generated form returns a StringEqualityTypeResult with the option methods and passes the chosen options to the method. The options also describe the compared value in the failure message, e.g. "has title starting with "Intro" ignoring case for at least 2 items". When the options are prepared and the expected value is validated The generated constraints override OnEvaluating of GeneratedCollectionConstraint<TCollection, TItem> and GeneratedAsyncCollectionConstraint<TItem>, which is called when an evaluation starts, before the collection is read. There they get the options of the evaluation and validate the expected value, so that an unusable value, e.g. an invalid regex pattern, is rejected also for an empty collection and names the parameter of the expectation, e.g. unexpected for the NegatedName.

The failure message lists the items with their formatter. To show something else for them, e.g. a wrapper that a formatter of your own formats, name a static method in the same class in FormattedItem. It takes the item, which can be null for a reference type, and its result stands for the item in the listed items and in the collection: [GenerateCollectionExpectation("AreLongerThan", "is longer than {minimum}", "are longer than {minimum}", FormattedItem = nameof(ToTitle))] private static bool IsLongerThan(Track track, TimeSpan minimum) => track.Duration > minimum; private static string? ToTitle(Track? track) => track?.Title;
A method that the generator cannot turn into an expectation is reported as an error, see the expectation generator.

An extension can run code before its first expectation, support a test framework of its own and read the running test. This page also shows how the test project passes values and code to your extension before the first test. Namespaces used on this page using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis; using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; using aweXpect.Core.Adapters; using aweXpect.Core.Extending; using aweXpect.Formatting;

An extension often has to run code once before its first expectation is evaluated, e.g. to register a value formatter. Use a module initializer, which runs before any other code of your assembly, i.e. when a test first uses the extension. In a class library, the attribute triggers the warning CA2255, so suppress it as shown: namespace MusicStore { internal static class MusicStoreInitializer { #pragma warning disable CA2255 // The initializer of a class library is intended here [ModuleInitializer] internal static void Initialize() => ValueFormatter.Register(new TrackFormatter()); #pragma warning restore CA2255 } } ModuleInitializerAttribute is missing in netstandard2.0 and net48: declare it in your own package there, see polyfills for older targets.

aweXpect reports a failed, skipped or inconclusive expectation by throwing the exception of the test framework. For MSTest, NUnit, TUnit and xUnit (v2 and v3), the aweXpect package generates an adapter into the test project and registers it (test frameworks lists the exceptions it throws). To support another test framework, implement ITestFrameworkAdapter and register it with TestFrameworkRegistry.Register from a module initializer in the test project itself, as the generated adapters are. A module initializer only runs when its assembly is first used, and the tests never use an assembly that only contains an adapter, so a registration in a separate package would never run: namespace MyTests { internal sealed class MyTestFrameworkAdapter : ITestFrameworkAdapter { public bool IsAvailable => true; public void Skip(string message) => throw new MyTestSkippedException(message); public void Fail(string message) => throw new MyTestFailedException(message); public void Fail(string message, Exception innerException) => throw new MyTestFailedException(message, innerException); public void Inconclusive(string message) => throw new MyTestInconclusiveException(message); public bool TryGetCurrentTest([NotNullWhen(true)] out RunningTest? currentTest) { MyTestContext? context = MyTestContext.Current; currentTest = context is null ? null : new RunningTest(new TestIdentity(context.ClassName, context.ClassArguments, context.MethodName, context.Arguments), context.Id, context.DisplayName, context.RetryCount); return currentTest is not null; } public bool TryGetCancellationToken(out CancellationToken cancellationToken) { MyTestContext? context = MyTestContext.Current; cancellationToken = context?.CancellationToken ?? CancellationToken.None; return context is not null; } // The test framework cannot attach files to the result of a test. public bool TryAddAttachment(string filePath, string? description) => false; } internal static class MyTestFrameworkRegistration { #pragma warning disable CA2255 // A test project is a class library, too [ModuleInitializer] internal static void Register() => TestFrameworkRegistry.Register(new MyTestFrameworkAdapter()); #pragma warning restore CA2255 } } The adapter is resolved once, when the first expectation is created or a value is first formatted with Format.Formatter, so register it before that. Availability, precedence and fallbacks An adapter whose IsAvailable is false is ignored, e.g. when the test framework it throws for is not loaded. By default, Register replaces an adapter that was registered before. With overwrite: false, as the generated registrations use it, the adapter is only used when no other one was registered, so an explicit registration always wins, independent of the order in which the module initializers run. Without any registration, aweXpect throws its own FailException, SkipException or InconclusiveException. Only below .NET 8, e.g. on .NET Framework, it first scans the loaded assemblies for a type that implements ITestFrameworkAdapter, see settings. The generated registration is a module initializer, which needs C# 9 or later. On .NET 8 or later, a test project with an older <LangVersion> has to register the generated adapter itself, which the warning aweXpect2002 points out.

The TryGetCurrentTest of an adapter returns the RunningTest, or false when its test framework does not expose it. Its Identity holds what identifies the test in every run: the full name of the test class and its arguments, the name of the test method and the arguments of the test case. When the test framework reports them, the RunningTest also holds the Id and the DisplayName of the test case and its RetryAttempt, which counts the runs of the test before, e.g. by a retry: 0 for the first run. The Id is only unique within one test run, so it does not belong in a persisted name. An extension reads the running test with TestFrameworkRegistry.TryGetCurrentTest, e.g. to tell the cases of a parameterized test apart, as aweXpect.Snapshots does with NamedAfterTestArguments: internal static class TrackCaseNames { internal static string? GetCaseName() => TestFrameworkRegistry.TryGetCurrentTest(out RunningTest? currentTest) && currentTest.Identity.Arguments.Count > 0 ? string.Join("_", currentTest.Identity.Arguments) : null; } It returns false when the test framework does not expose the running test, or when no test is running, e.g. in a setup of the whole assembly. Handle that case, as not every test framework exposes the running test; the test frameworks page lists what each of them supports. TestFrameworkRegistry.TryGetCancellationToken returns the token with which the test framework cancels the running test. Expectations only observe it when Settings().TestCancellation is set to TestCancellation.FromCancellationToken(…) with it, see time and cancellation. TestFrameworkRegistry.TryAddAttachment(filePath, description) attaches a file to the result of the running test, as aweXpect.Snapshots does with a recorded mismatch when AttachPendingFiles is set: internal static class PlaylistReports { internal static void Attach(string reportFile) => _ = TestFrameworkRegistry.TryAddAttachment(reportFile, "The report of the test"); } Both return false when the test framework does not support it, no test is running or the test framework fails, e.g. because the file does not exist. Like TryGetCurrentTest, they never throw: the registry also returns false when an adapter throws, but an adapter of your own should still return false instead. MSTest, NUnit and TUnit only read the file when the test ends, so it must still exist then.

Some extensions need values that the build of the test project records, e.g. its directory, or have to run code before the first test, e.g. to add a reporter, although no test uses their assembly before. Instead of scanning the loaded assemblies, let the source generator of aweXpect.Core emit a module initializer into the test project. The build targets of your package (in its buildTransitive folder) only pass names to it, in two MSBuild properties: AweXpectRegisteredMetadataKeys: the keys of the AssemblyMetadataAttributes of the test project whose values are registered in ExtensionRegistry. AweXpectModuleInitializers: the static methods without parameters, accessible from the test project, that are called afterwards, so that they can already read the registered values. Both are lists separated by , or ;.
