expected total free space HasAvailableFreeSpace has the expected available free space Expectations for IFileVersionInfo: Expectation Negated Summary HasCompanyName, HasFileMajorPart, IsDebug, … IsNotDebug, … one expectation per property The samples on this page use the following file system: using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package using static aweXpect.Expect; MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(o => o.SimulatingOperatingSystem(SimulationMode.Windows)); fileSystem.WithDrive("D:", d => d.SetTotalSize(2048)); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("beatles/abbey-road"); fileSystem.Directory.CreateDirectory("beatles/revolver"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("beatles/abbey-road/something.txt", "something"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("let-it-be.txt", "let it be"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("let-it-be-remastered.txt", "LET IT BE"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("hey-jude.txt", "hey jude"); fileSystem.File.SetAttributes("hey-jude.txt", FileAttributes.ReadOnly);

You can verify that a file, directory or drive exists in an IFileSystem, or that it does not: await That(fileSystem).HasDirectory("beatles/abbey-road"); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt"); await That(fileSystem).HasDrive("D:\\"); await That(fileSystem).DoesNotHaveDirectory("beatles/white-album"); await That(fileSystem).DoesNotHaveFile("yesterday.txt"); await That(fileSystem).DoesNotHaveDrive("E:\\"); For example, That(fileSystem).HasFile("yesterday.txt") fails with: Failure message Expected that fileSystem has file "yesterday.txt", but it did not exist HasDrive matches the drive name case-insensitively against IFileSystem.DriveInfo.GetDrives(). UNC drives are not returned by GetDrives() and are therefore not supported by HasDrive.

You can verify the content of the file found by HasFile(path): await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithContent("LET IT BE").IgnoringCase(); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithContent().NotEqualTo("let it go"); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithContent(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("let it be")); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WhoseContent(c => c.StartsWith("let it")); The string content supports the same options as comparing strings, and WhoseContent accepts any string expectation. When the content differs, the failure message shows where and includes the file content: Failure message Expected that fileSystem has file "let-it-be.txt" with content equal to "let it go", but it was "let it be", which differs at index 7: ↓ (actual) "let it be" "let it go" ↑ (expected) File content: let it be You can also compare the content with another file on the same file system: await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithContent().SameAs("let-it-be-remastered.txt").IgnoringCase(); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithContent().NotSameAs("hey-jude.txt"); You can verify the timestamps of the file, and widen the comparison to a window with .Within(tolerance): await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithCreationTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithLastAccessTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").WithLastWriteTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds());

You can verify the files and subdirectories of the directory found by HasDirectory(path): await That(fileSystem).HasDirectory("beatles").WithDirectories(d => d.HasCount().EqualTo(2)); await That(fileSystem).HasDirectory("beatles/abbey-road").WithFiles(f => f .All().ComplyWith(x => x.HasContent("SOMETHING").IgnoringCase()));

HasFile, HasDirectory and HasDrive each have a .Which property that continues with the found IFileInfo, IDirectoryInfo or IDriveInfo, so that the expectations of the following sections can be used in the same chain: await That(fileSystem).HasFile("let-it-be.txt").Which.HasLength(9).And.HasContent("let it be"); await That(fileSystem).HasDirectory("beatles/revolver").Which.IsEmpty(); await That(fileSystem).HasDrive("D:\\").Which.IsReady().And.HasDriveFormat("NTFS");
documents.s: Continuing with the file, directory or drive

documents.t: You can verify the properties of an IFileInfo: IFileInfo fileInfo = fileSystem.FileInfo.New("let-it-be.txt"); IFileInfo readOnlyFileInfo = fileSystem.FileInfo.New("hey-jude.txt"); await That(fileInfo).Exists(); await That(fileSystem.FileInfo.New("yesterday.txt")).DoesNotExist(); await That(fileInfo).HasName("let-it-be.txt"); await That(fileInfo).HasExtension(".txt"); await That(fileInfo).HasLength(9); await That(readOnlyFileInfo).IsReadOnly(); await That(fileInfo).IsNotReadOnly(); await That(readOnlyFileInfo).HasAttribute(FileAttributes.ReadOnly); await That(fileInfo).DoesNotHaveAttribute(FileAttributes.ReadOnly); await That(fileInfo).HasCreationTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); await That(fileInfo).HasLastAccessTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); await That(fileInfo).HasLastWriteTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); For example, That(fileInfo).HasLength(10) fails with: Failure message Expected that fileInfo has length 10, but it was 9 You can verify the content of the file, or compare it with another file on the same file system, like with HasFile: await That(fileInfo).HasContent("let it be"); await That(fileInfo).HasContent(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("let it be")); await That(fileInfo).HasContent().NotEqualTo("let it go"); await That(fileInfo).HasContent().SameAs("let-it-be-remastered.txt").IgnoringCase(); await That(fileInfo).HasContent().NotSameAs("hey-jude.txt"); HasAttribute and DoesNotHaveAttribute check whether the flag is contained, so FileAttributes.ReadOnly | FileAttributes.Hidden satisfies HasAttribute(FileAttributes.ReadOnly). The empty (default) value throws an ArgumentException, because it would be contained in every value. .NET 10 or later WhoseParent continues with the containing directory, so that the directory expectations can be used: IFileInfo something = fileSystem.FileInfo.New("beatles/abbey-road/something.txt"); await That(something).WhoseParent.HasName("abbey-road").And.IsNotEmpty();

You can verify the properties of an IDirectoryInfo: IDirectoryInfo dirInfo = fileSystem.DirectoryInfo.New("beatles"); IDirectoryInfo emptyDirInfo = fileSystem.DirectoryInfo.New("beatles/revolver"); await That(dirInfo).Exists(); await That(fileSystem.DirectoryInfo.New("beatles/white-album")).DoesNotExist(); await That(dirInfo).HasName("beatles"); await That(emptyDirInfo).IsEmpty(); await That(dirInfo).IsNotEmpty(); await That(dirInfo).HasFile("abbey-road/something.txt"); await That(dirInfo).DoesNotHaveFile("abbey-road/yesterday.txt"); await That(dirInfo).HasDirectory("abbey-road").Which.HasFile("something.txt"); await That(dirInfo).DoesNotHaveDirectory("white-album"); await That(dirInfo).HasAttribute(FileAttributes.Directory); await That(dirInfo).DoesNotHaveAttribute(FileAttributes.Hidden); await That(dirInfo).HasCreationTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); await That(dirInfo).HasLastAccessTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); await That(dirInfo).HasLastWriteTime(DateTime.Now).Within(1.Seconds()); HasFile and HasDirectory resolve the path relative to the directory and continue like on the file system, so .WithContent(…), .WithLastWriteTime(…), .Which etc. work as well. .NET 10 or later WhoseParent continues with the parent directory: await That(emptyDirInfo).WhoseParent.HasName("beatles");

You can verify the properties of an IDriveInfo: IDriveInfo driveInfo = fileSystem.DriveInfo.New("D:"); await That(driveInfo).HasAvailableFreeSpace(2048); await That(driveInfo).HasTotalSize(2048).And.HasTotalFreeSpace(2048); await That(driveInfo).HasDriveFormat("NTFS"); await That(driveInfo).HasDriveType(DriveType.Fixed); await That(driveInfo).HasName(driveInfo.Name).And.HasVolumeLabel(driveInfo.VolumeLabel); await That(driveInfo).IsReady();

You can verify an IFileVersionInfo obtained via MockFileSystem.FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo. Its values come from MockFileSystem.WithFileVersionInfo(glob, builder): fileSystem.WithFileVersionInfo("*.dll", v => v .SetCompanyName("Apple Corps") .SetProductName("Abbey Road") .SetFileVersion("1.9.6.9") .SetIsDebug(true)); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("AbbeyRoad.dll", ""); IFileVersionInfo info = fileSystem.FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo("AbbeyRoad.dll"); await That(info).HasCompanyName("Apple Corps").And.HasProductName("Abbey Road"); await That(info).HasFileVersion("1.9.6.9").And.HasFileMajorPart(1); await That(info).IsDebug().And.IsNotPreRelease(); For example, That(info).HasCompanyName("EMI") fails with: Failure message Expected that info has company name equal to "EMI", but it was "Apple Corps", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "Apple Corps" "EMI" ↑ (expected) Every IFileVersionInfo property has its own expectation: Has…(string) for the strings, Has…(int) for the version parts and an Is…() / IsNot…() pair for the booleans. Expectations per property Property Expectation Comments HasComments(string) CompanyName HasCompanyName(string) FileDescription HasFileDescription(string) FileName HasFileName(string) FileVersion HasFileVersion(string) InternalName HasInternalName(string) Language HasLanguage(string) LegalCopyright HasLegalCopyright(string) LegalTrademarks HasLegalTrademarks(string) OriginalFilename HasOriginalFilename(string) PrivateBuild HasPrivateBuild(string) ProductName HasProductName(string) ProductVersion HasProductVersion(string) SpecialBuild HasSpecialBuild(string) FileBuildPart HasFileBuildPart(int) FileMajorPart HasFileMajorPart(int) FileMinorPart HasFileMinorPart(int) FilePrivatePart HasFilePrivatePart(int) ProductBuildPart HasProductBuildPart(int) ProductMajorPart HasProductMajorPart(int) ProductMinorPart HasProductMinorPart(int) ProductPrivatePart HasProductPrivatePart(int) IsDebug IsDebug() / IsNotDebug() IsPatched IsPatched() / IsNotPatched() IsPreRelease IsPreRelease() / IsNotPreRelease() IsPrivateBuild IsPrivateBuild() / IsNotPrivateBuild() IsSpecialBuild IsSpecialBuild() / IsNotSpecialBuild()

Describes the possible expectations for the changes the code under test made to a MockFileSystem: the notifications it raised, the events of a single watcher, and the method calls and property accesses it recorded. Expectation Negated Summary TriggeredNotification DidNotTriggerNotification the MockFileSystem raised a matching notification Triggered DidNotTrigger the IFileSystemWatcher raised a matching event HasChangeType DoesNotHaveChangeType the change has the change type flag HasFileSystemType DoesNotHaveFileSystemType the change has the file system type flag HasNotifyFilters DoesNotHaveNotifyFilters the change has the notify filters flag HasName the change has the expected name HasPath the change has the expected path HasOldName the renamed change has the expected old name HasOldPath the renamed change has the expected old path Recorded .Never() the IFileSystemStatistics recorded a method call or property access The samples on this page use the following file system and watcher: using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package using static aweXpect.Expect; MockFileSystem fileSystem = new(); fileSystem.InitializeIn("/music"); using IFileSystemWatcher watcher = fileSystem.FileSystemWatcher.New("/music"); watcher.EnableRaisingEvents = true; fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("let-it-be.txt", "let it be"); fileSystem.File.WriteAllText("scrambled-eggs.txt", "scrambled eggs"); fileSystem.File.Move("scrambled-eggs.txt", "yesterday.txt");

A MockFileSystem raises notifications when files or directories change. You can verify that the code under test triggered a notification, or that it did not: await That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification(); await That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification(c => c.Name == "let-it-be.txt"); await That(fileSystem).DidNotTriggerNotification(c => c.Name == "free-as-a-bird.txt"); Both accept a quantifier (AtLeast, AtMost, Exactly, Between, Never, Once; at least once by default) to verify how often the notification was triggered, and a .Matching(c => …) filter with the change description expectations for each notification: await That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification(c => c.ChangeType == WatcherChangeTypes.Renamed).Once(); await That(fileSystem) .TriggeredNotification() .Matching(c => c.HasName("let-it-be.txt").And.HasChangeType(WatcherChangeTypes.Created)) .Exactly(1.Times()); Without .Within(timeout), the expectations check only the notifications triggered so far and do not wait. With .Within(timeout), they also wait for asynchronous notifications, like waiting for events: TriggeredNotification completes as soon as the quantifier is decided, so only an upper bound like .Never() or .AtMost(…) waits for the full timeout, and DidNotTriggerNotification waits for the full timeout and fails as soon as a matching notification is triggered. .Within(Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan) waits until the quantifier is decided. _ = Task.Run(() => fileSystem.File.Delete("let-it-be.txt")); await That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification(c => c.ChangeType == WatcherChangeTypes.Deleted) .Within(100.Milliseconds()); await That(fileSystem).DidNotTriggerNotification(c => c.Name == "free-as-a-bird.txt") .Within(100.Milliseconds()); For example, That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification(c => c.Name == "free-as-a-bird.txt").Within(100.Milliseconds()) fails with: Failure message Expected that fileSystem has triggered a notification matching c => c.Name == "free-as-a-bird.txt" at least once within 0:00.100, but it was not triggered A timeout of the evaluation (e.g. .WithTimeout(…)) that is not shorter than .Within(timeout) lets the notifications received until then decide; a cancellation before that leaves the expectation inconclusive. Notification history These expectations replay the notification history of the MockFileSystem. They throw on a file system created with new MockFileSystem(o => o.WithoutNotificationHistory()).

You can verify the events of a single IFileSystemWatcher, similar to the events of any other object. The watcher must come from a MockFileSystem and have EnableRaisingEvents set to true. Only events of this watcher count; events of other watchers on the same MockFileSystem are ignored. await That(watcher).Triggered().Within(1.Seconds()); await That(watcher).Triggered(c => c.Name == "let-it-be.txt").Within(1.Seconds()); await That(watcher).DidNotTrigger(c => c.Name == "free-as-a-bird.txt").Within(100.Milliseconds()); The mock raises the events of a watcher asynchronously, like a real FileSystemWatcher, so an event of a change that just completed may not be raised yet. Without .Within(timeout), only the events raised so far count; use it to wait for them. Triggered() completes as soon as a matching event is raised, so a generous timeout only costs time when the expectation fails. Triggered and DidNotTrigger support the same quantifiers, .Within(timeout) and .Matching(c => …) filter as the notification expectations: await That(watcher) .Triggered() .Matching(c => c.HasName("let-it-be.txt").And.HasChangeType(WatcherChangeTypes.Created)) .Exactly(1.Times()) .Within(1.Seconds());

You can verify a single ChangeDescription, e.g. a notification in .Matching(…) or the event of a watcher: await That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification().Matching(change => change .HasChangeType(WatcherChangeTypes.Created).And .DoesNotHaveChangeType(WatcherChangeTypes.Deleted).And .HasFileSystemType(FileSystemTypes.File).And .HasNotifyFilters(NotifyFilters.FileName).And .HasName("let-it-be.txt").And .HasPath(fileSystem.Path.GetFullPath("let-it-be.txt"))); await That(fileSystem).TriggeredNotification().Matching(renamedChange => renamedChange .HasChangeType(WatcherChangeTypes.Renamed).And .HasOldName("scrambled-eggs.txt").And .HasOldPath(fileSystem.Path.GetFullPath("scrambled-eggs.txt"))); HasChangeType, HasFileSystemType and HasNotifyFilters check whether the flag is contained, so a LastWrite | FileName change satisfies HasNotifyFilters(NotifyFilters.LastWrite). The empty (default) value throws an ArgumentException, because it would be contained in every value.

MockFileSystem.Statistics records every method call and property access on the mock. You can verify what the code under test called with .Recorded(), which mirrors the IFileSystem API: await That(fileSystem.Statistics).Recorded().File.WriteAllText().Twice(); await That(fileSystem.Statistics).Recorded().File.WriteAllText(path: p => p == "let-it-be.txt").Once(); await That(fileSystem.Statistics).Recorded().File.Copy().Never(); For example, That(fileSystem.Statistics).Recorded().File.WriteAllText().Once() fails with: Failure message Expected that fileSystem.Statistics has recorded a call to File.WriteAllText exactly once, but it was recorded 2 times The mirror has one entry per IFileSystem member (.File, .Directory, .FileInfo[path], .DirectoryInfo[path], .DriveInfo, .FileStream, .FileSystemWatcher, .FileVersionInfo, .Path), with one method per underlying API and an indexer ([path]) for the instances of a path. Every result supports the quantifiers Once, Twice, Never, Exactly, AtLeast, AtMost, Between, … and verifies at least one call without a quantifier. note As for every quantifier in this package, only one can be specified: chaining two, e.g. .Once().Twice(), throws an InvalidOperationException; use Between(minimum).And(maximum) for a range. Property reads and writes are recorded with .Get() and .Set(): fileSystem.FileInfo.New("yesterday.txt").IsReadOnly = true; await That(fileSystem.Statistics).Recorded().FileInfo["yesterday.txt"].IsReadOnly.Set().Once(); await That(fileSystem.Statistics).Recorded().FileInfo["yesterday.txt"].IsReadOnly.Get().Never(); Each parameter of a mirror method is an optional Func<T, bool> predicate that is matched by position against the recorded arguments. How the predicates are matched by position Without a predicate (or with null) the position is skipped and every overload matches, so .File.Open() counts all Open calls regardless of their arguments. A predicate at a position beyond the number of parameters of an overload excludes that overload, so filtering recursive on Directory.Delete only matches the overload with two parameters. A predicate whose type differs from the recorded type at that position excludes that overload, so filtering searchOption on Directory.EnumerateDirectories never matches the EnumerationOptions overload. A few methods cannot be filtered completely by position, because two of their overloads have different types at the same position (File.Open / FileInfo.Open with FileStreamOptions, FileSystemWatcher.WaitForChanged with TimeSpan).

Describes the possible expectations for the timers of a MockTimeSystem. Expectation Negated Summary Executed .Never() the timer callback was executed The samples on this page use the following timer: using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package using static aweXpect.Expect; MockTimeSystem timeSystem = new(); ITimerMock timer = (ITimerMock)timeSystem.Timer.New(_ => { }, null, TimeSpan.Zero, 10.Milliseconds());

A MockTimeSystem creates timers as ITimerMock. You can verify how often the timer callback was executed without blocking the test thread: await That(timer).Executed().AtLeast(3.Times()).Within(5.Seconds()); Executed() accepts a quantifier (AtLeast, AtMost, Exactly, Between, Never, Once; at least once by default). Without .Within(timeout), it checks ITimerMock.ExecutionCount once and does not wait. With .Within(timeout), it checks the count again until the quantifier is decided or the timeout expires, so an upper bound like .Never() or .AtMost(…) waits for the full timeout. Like for a condition, the count is checked every DefaultCheckInterval, or in the interval of .CheckEvery(interval): await That(timer).Executed().AtLeast(3.Times()).Within(5.Seconds()).CheckEvery(10.Milliseconds()); A timeout of the evaluation (e.g. .WithTimeout(…)) that is not shorter than .Within(timeout) lets the last check decide; a cancellation before that leaves the expectation inconclusive. For example, for a timer that never fires, That(timer).Executed().AtLeast(3.Times()).Within(100.Milliseconds()) fails with: Failure message Expected that timer has executed at least 3 times within 0:00.100, but it was not executed
aweXpect.Web extends aweXpect with expectations for HttpRequestMessage, HttpResponseMessage, Uri and IPAddress, e.g. to verify the responses of an HttpClient.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Web --prerelease <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Web" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Web" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Web" /> Latest version: 4.0.0-pre.3 The package brings Expect.That with it, but not the expectations for strings, numbers or collections, so reference aweXpect as well. The expectations live in the namespace aweXpect, so using aweXpect; is all you need; only the customization lives in aweXpect.Web. The examples write That(...) instead of Expect.That(...), which needs using static aweXpect.Expect; (see Getting started).

HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); // verify the status code, either the exact value or its category await That(response).HasStatusCode().Success(); // verify the media type and the headers of the response await That(response).HasContentType("application/json"); await That(response).HasHeader("Cache-Control").WithValue("must-revalidate, max-age=0, private"); // verify the content of the response await That(response).HasContent("*Let It Be*").AsWildcard(); A failing expectation on a request or response includes the formatted HTTP request and response. If the test server returned the track, HasStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.NotFound) would fail with: Failure message Expected that response has status code equal to 404 NotFound, but it had status code 200 OK HTTP-Request: GET http://localhost/tracks/1 HTTP/1.1 HTTP-Response: 200 OK HTTP/1.1 x-vendor: VENDOR Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 51 { "id": 1, "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles" }

Expectations for HttpRequestMessage: Expectation Negated Summary HasMethod DoesNotHaveMethod has the expected HTTP method HasRequestUri DoesNotHaveRequestUri has the expected request URI HasHeader DoesNotHaveHeader has a header, optionally with a value HasContentType DoesNotHaveContentType has the expected media type HasContent DoesNotHaveContent has the expected string content Expectations for HttpResponseMessage: Expectation Negated Summary HasStatusCode DoesNotHaveStatusCode has the expected status code or status category HasHeader DoesNotHaveHeader has a header, optionally with a value HasContentType DoesNotHaveContentType has the expected media type HasContent DoesNotHaveContent has the expected string content HasProblemDetailsContent use DoesNotHaveContentType has a ProblemDetails content HasRequestMessage the request message meets nested expectations Expectations for Uri: Expectation Negated Summary IsAbsolute IsNotAbsolute an absolute URI IsFile IsNotFile a file URI IsLoopback IsNotLoopback references the local host IsUnc IsNotUnc a UNC path HasDefaultPort DoesNotHaveDefaultPort uses the default port of its scheme HasPort use HasPort().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected port HasScheme use HasScheme().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected scheme HasHost use HasHost().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected host HasPath use HasPath().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected path HasFragment use HasFragment().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected fragment IsBaseOf IsNotBaseOf a base URI of the expected URI HasQueryParameter DoesNotHaveQueryParameter has a query parameter, optionally with a value Expectations for IPAddress: Expectation Negated Summary IsIPv4 IsNotIPv4 an IPv4 address IsIPv6 IsNotIPv6 an IPv6 address IsLoopback IsNotLoopback a loopback address IsInSubnet IsNotInSubnet in the expected subnet IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected address, optionally ignoring mapping

Set a value under Customize.aweXpect.Web() for the current async flow, or under Customize.aweXpect.Global.Web() for all tests. Value Default Summary ContentProcessors JsonContentProcessor, StringContentProcessor, BinaryContentProcessor format the content of requests and responses in failure messages

HTTP requests and responses: method, request URI, headers, content type and content of an HttpRequestMessage, and status code, headers, content type, content, problem details and the request message of an HttpResponseMessage URIs: kind, port, scheme, host, path, fragment, base URI and query parameters of a Uri IP addresses: IPv4, IPv6, loopback, subnet membership and equality of an IPAddress Customization: formatting the request and response content in failure messages

These benchmarks compare the happy-path overhead of aweXpect.Web (passing assertions, the dominant case in a healthy test suite) against the equivalent FluentAssertions calls. Methodology Suite: HappyCaseBenchmarks driven by BenchmarkDotNet. Job: MediumRun with the in-process toolchain. Runner: ubuntu-latest GitHub Actions agent, refreshed on every push to main. FluentAssertions has no expectations on HttpResponseMessage or Uri, so its benchmarks do what a FluentAssertions user writes instead, e.g. read the content as a string. Each tab shows the latest measured time and allocated memory; bars are scaled within the row so length corresponds to magnitude. Lower is better. Set a value under Customize.aweXpect.Web() for the current async flow, or under Customize.aweXpect.Global.Web() for all tests. Value Default Summary ContentProcessors JsonContentProcessor, StringContentProcessor, BinaryContentProcessor format the content of requests and responses in failure messages

The failure messages include the content of the request and the response. Each content is formatted by the first content processor that can handle it: by default JSON is indented, text is shown as is, and audio, image, video and PDF content is summarized with its media type and length. You can change the processors, e.g. with your own IContentProcessor: using aweXpect.Customization; using aweXpect.Web; using aweXpect.Web.ContentProcessors; using (Customize.aweXpect.Web().ContentProcessors.Set([ new MyCsvContentProcessor(), new JsonContentProcessor(), new StringContentProcessor(), new BinaryContentProcessor(), ])) { // formats CSV content with the custom processor }

Describes the possible expectations for HttpRequestMessage and HttpResponseMessage. Expectations for HttpRequestMessage: Expectation Negated Summary HasMethod DoesNotHaveMethod has the expected HTTP method HasRequestUri DoesNotHaveRequestUri has the expected request URI HasHeader DoesNotHaveHeader has a header, optionally with a value HasContentType DoesNotHaveContentType has the expected media type HasContent DoesNotHaveContent has the expected string content Expectations for HttpResponseMessage: Expectation Negated Summary HasStatusCode DoesNotHaveStatusCode has the expected status code or status category HasHeader DoesNotHaveHeader has a header, optionally with a value HasContentType DoesNotHaveContentType has the expected media type HasContent DoesNotHaveContent has the expected string content HasProblemDetailsContent use DoesNotHaveContentType has a ProblemDetails content HasRequestMessage the request message meets nested expectations

You can verify that the HttpRequestMessage has the expected method, or that it does not have it: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Get, "https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(request).HasMethod(HttpMethod.Get); await That(request).DoesNotHaveMethod(HttpMethod.Delete);

You can verify that the HttpRequestMessage has the expected request URI, or that it does not have it: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Get, "https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(request).HasRequestUri("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(request).HasRequestUri(new Uri("https://music.example.com/tracks/1")); await That(request).DoesNotHaveRequestUri("https://music.example.com/admin"); Scheme and host are compared ignoring case; path, query and fragment are case-sensitive, unless you add .IgnoringCase(): await That(request).HasRequestUri("https://music.example.com/Tracks/1").IgnoringCase(); await That(request).DoesNotHaveRequestUri("https://music.example.com/Admin").IgnoringCase(); The expected request URI is compared as a URI, so it supports no match types. To verify parts of the request URI, e.g. with a wildcard or a prefix, add expectations on the request URI with the URI expectations: await That(request).HasRequestUri(uri => uri .HasHost().EqualTo("music.example.com").And .HasPath().StartingWith("/tracks/")); await That(request).HasRequestUri(uri => uri.HasPath("/tracks/*").AsWildcard()); To negate the nested expectations, use DoesNotComplyWith(it => it.HasRequestUri(uri => ...)).

You can verify that the HttpRequestMessage has a header, optionally with the expected value, or that it does not have it: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Get, "https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); request.Headers.Add("Accept", "application/json"); await That(request).HasHeader("Accept"); await That(request).HasHeader("Accept").WithValue("application/json"); await That(request).HasHeader("Accept").WithValue("application/*").AsWildcard(); await That(request).DoesNotHaveHeader("Authorization"); The headers of the content are included, so you can also verify headers like Content-Type, Content-Length or Content-Disposition. Their value is the raw header value, e.g. application/json; charset=utf-8, so use HasContentType to verify the media type. WithValue supports the same string options and match types as comparing strings, e.g. .WithValue("application").AsPrefix().IgnoringCase(). When the header has multiple values, WithValues verifies that it has exactly these values in the same order: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Get, "https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); request.Headers.Add("Accept", ["application/json", "text/plain"]); await That(request).HasHeader("Accept").WithValues("application/json", "text/plain"); WithValues supports the same string options, match types and collection options as comparing string collections, e.g. .WithValues("text/plain", "application/json").InAnyOrder().IgnoringCase(). You can also add expectations on the header value or on all of its values: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Get, "https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); request.Headers.Add("Accept-Encoding", ["gzip", "deflate"]); await That(request).HasHeader("Accept-Encoding") .WhoseValues(values => values.Contains("gzip")); The failure message shows the difference and the request: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Get, "https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); request.Headers.Add("Cache-Control", "no-cache"); await That(request).HasHeader("Cache-Control").WithValue("max-age=0"); Failure message Expected that request has a "Cache-Control" header whose value is equal to "max-age=0", but it had header value "no-cache", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "no-cache" "max-age=0" ↑ (expected) HTTP-Request: GET https://music.example.com/tracks/1 HTTP/1.1 Cache-Control: no-cache

You can verify the media type in the Content-Type header of the HttpRequestMessage: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Post, "https://music.example.com/tracks") { Content = new StringContent("{\"title\": \"Let It Be\"}", Encoding.UTF8, "application/json"), }; await That(request).HasContentType("application/json"); await That(request).HasContentType("application/*").AsWildcard(); await That(request).DoesNotHaveContentType("text/html"); The media type supports the same string options and match types as comparing strings. As RFC 9110 defines the media type as case-insensitive, it is compared ignoring case by default, also with a match type. Add .IgnoringCase(false) to compare it case-sensitively, which a .Using(comparer) or a match type of your own that cannot ignore the casing needs as well. A request without content or without a Content-Type header does not have the unexpected media type.

You can verify that the HttpRequestMessage has the expected string content, or that it does not have it: HttpRequestMessage request = new(HttpMethod.Post, "https://music.example.com/tracks") { Content = new StringContent("{\"title\": \"Let It Be\"}"), }; await That(request).HasContent("*Let It Be*").AsWildcard(); await That(request).HasContent(content => content.Contains("Let It Be")); await That(request).DoesNotHaveContent(""); The content supports the same string options and match types as comparing strings. A request without content has an empty content, like a response, as HTTP does not distinguish a missing body from an empty one. To negate the nested expectations, use DoesNotComplyWith(it => it.HasContent(content => ...)).

You can verify the status code of the HttpResponseMessage, either the exact value or its category: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.OK); await That(response).DoesNotHaveStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.NotFound); await That(response).HasStatusCode().EqualTo(HttpStatusCode.OK); await That(response).HasStatusCode().NotEqualTo(HttpStatusCode.NotFound); await That(response).HasStatusCode().Success(); The categories are Success() (2xx), Redirection() (3xx), ClientError() (4xx), ServerError() (5xx) and Error() (4xx or 5xx). Combine them with .Or to allow several: StringContent track = new("""{"title": "Let It Be"}"""); HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.PostAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks", track); await That(response).HasStatusCode().ClientError().Or.HasStatusCode().ServerError(); A failing expectation against a test server HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasStatusCode(HttpStatusCode.NotFound); fails with the request and the response: Failure message Expected that response has status code equal to 404 NotFound, but it had status code 200 OK HTTP-Request: GET http://localhost/tracks/1 HTTP/1.1 HTTP-Response: 200 OK HTTP/1.1 x-vendor: VENDOR Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 51 { "id": 1, "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles" }

You can verify that the HttpResponseMessage has a header, optionally with the expected value, or that it does not have it: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasHeader("Cache-Control"); await That(response).HasHeader("Cache-Control").WithValue("must-revalidate, max-age=0, private"); await That(response).HasHeader("Cache-Control").WithValue("*max-age=0*").AsWildcard(); await That(response).DoesNotHaveHeader("Set-Cookie"); The headers of the content are included, so you can also verify headers like Content-Type, Content-Length or Content-Disposition. Their value is the raw header value, e.g. application/json; charset=utf-8, so use HasContentType to verify the media type. WithValue supports the same string options and match types as comparing strings. When the header has multiple values, WithValues verifies that it has exactly these values in the same order: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasHeader("Vary").WithValues("Accept", "Accept-Encoding"); WithValues supports the same string options, match types and collection options as comparing string collections, e.g. .WithValues("text/plain", "application/json").InAnyOrder().IgnoringCase(). You can also add expectations on the header value or on all of its values: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasHeader("ETag") .WhoseValue(value => value.IsNotEmpty()); await That(response).HasHeader("Vary") .WhoseValues(values => values.Contains("Accept-Encoding")); Like WithValue, WhoseValue requires the header to have exactly one value, also when it is negated.

You can verify the media type in the Content-Type header of the HttpResponseMessage: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasContentType("application/json"); await That(response).HasContentType("application/*").AsWildcard(); await That(response).DoesNotHaveContentType("text/html"); As for a request, the media type is compared ignoring case by default, also with a match type; add .IgnoringCase(false) to compare it case-sensitively. A response without a Content-Type header does not have the unexpected media type. For example, expecting plain text from an endpoint that returns JSON HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasContentType("text/plain"); fails with the difference, the request and the response: Failure message Expected that response has a `Content-Type` header equal to "text/plain" ignoring case, but it had content type "application/json", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "application/json" "text/plain" ↑ (expected) HTTP-Request: GET http://localhost/tracks/1 HTTP/1.1 HTTP-Response: 200 OK HTTP/1.1 x-vendor: VENDOR Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8 Content-Length: 51 { "id": 1, "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles" }

You can verify that the HttpResponseMessage has the expected string content, or that it does not have it: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasContent("*Let It Be*").AsWildcard(); await That(response).HasContent(content => content.Contains("The Beatles")); await That(response).DoesNotHaveContent("*error*").AsWildcard().IgnoringCase(); The content supports the same string options and match types as comparing strings. To negate the nested expectations, use DoesNotComplyWith(it => it.HasContent(content => ...)). With aweXpect.Json, the nested expectations can also verify JSON content: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasContent(content => content .IsValidJsonMatching(new { title = "Let It Be", artist = "The Beatles" }));

You can verify that the content of the HttpResponseMessage is a valid ProblemDetails object, optionally with the expected type, title, status, detail and instance: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/42"); await That(response) .HasProblemDetailsContent("https://httpstatuses.com/404") .WithTitle("Track not found") .WithStatus(404) .WithInstance("/tracks/42"); A content without a type member has the type "about:blank", as defined in RFC 9457. The type, title, detail and instance support the same string options and match types as comparing strings. The options apply to the value specified right before them: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/42"); await That(response) .HasProblemDetailsContent("*/404").AsWildcard() .WithTitle("track not found").IgnoringCase() .WithInstance("/tracks/").AsPrefix(); To verify that a response is no problem details response, verify that it does not have the problem details media type: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).DoesNotHaveContentType("application/problem+json"); RFC 9457 identifies problem details by this media type, whereas the structural check of HasProblemDetailsContent accepts almost any JSON object, as all of its members are optional. Absent members A pattern, prefix or suffix fails for an absent member, also with DoesNotComplyWith, as there is no value to inspect.

You can add expectations on the HttpRequestMessage that led to the HttpResponseMessage: HttpResponseMessage response = await httpClient.GetAsync("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(response).HasRequestMessage(request => request .HasMethod(HttpMethod.Get).And .HasRequestUri("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"));

Describes the possible expectations for IPAddress. Expectation Negated Summary IsIPv4 IsNotIPv4 an IPv4 address IsIPv6 IsNotIPv6 an IPv6 address IsLoopback IsNotLoopback a loopback address IsInSubnet IsNotInSubnet in the expected subnet IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected address, optionally ignoring mapping

You can verify what kind of address the IPAddress is, or that it is not: IPAddress address = IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1"); await That(address).IsIPv4(); await That(address).IsNotIPv6(); await That(address).IsNotLoopback(); The address family decides between IPv4 and IPv6. An IPv4-mapped address like ::ffff:10.0.0.1 is an IPv6 address, so IPAddress address = IPAddress.Parse("::ffff:10.0.0.1"); await That(address).IsIPv4(); fails with: Failure message Expected that address is an IPv4 address, but it was ::ffff:10.0.0.1 For IsLoopback, an IPv4-mapped address is mapped to its IPv4 address first, so ::ffff:127.0.0.2 is a loopback address like 127.0.0.2 on every target framework. IsLoopback for a Uri relies on Uri.IsLoopback instead, which treats only [::ffff:127.0.0.1] of the IPv4-mapped addresses as loopback.

You can verify that the IPAddress is in a subnet given in CIDR notation, or that it is not: IPAddress address = IPAddress.Parse("192.168.0.1"); await That(address).IsInSubnet("192.168.0.0/16"); await That(address).IsNotInSubnet("10.0.0.0/8"); For example, await That(address).IsInSubnet("10.0.0.0/8"); fails with: Failure message Expected that address is in subnet 10.0.0.0/8, but it was 192.168.0.1 An IPv4 address is in an IPv6 subnet if its IPv4-mapped address is, and an IPv4-mapped address is in an IPv4 subnet if its IPv4 address is: await That(IPAddress.Parse("::ffff:10.0.0.1")).IsInSubnet("10.0.0.0/8"); await That(IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1")).IsInSubnet("::ffff:0:0/96");

You can verify that the IPAddress is equal to an expected address, or that it is not: IPAddress address = IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1"); await That(address).IsEqualTo(IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1")); await That(address).IsNotEqualTo(IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.2")); The comparison uses IPAddress.Equals, so an IPv4-mapped address like ::ffff:10.0.0.1 is not equal to 10.0.0.1. With IgnoringIPv4MappedToIPv6(), IPv4-mapped addresses on either side are mapped to IPv4 before comparing: IPAddress address = IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1"); await That(address).IsEqualTo(IPAddress.Parse("::ffff:10.0.0.1")).IgnoringIPv4MappedToIPv6(); Different addresses are still not equal, so IPAddress address = IPAddress.Parse("::ffff:10.0.0.2"); await That(address).IsEqualTo(IPAddress.Parse("10.0.0.1")).IgnoringIPv4MappedToIPv6(); fails with: Failure message Expected that address is equal to 10.0.0.1 ignoring IPv4-to-IPv6 mapping, but it was ::ffff:10.0.0.2 note The other options for comparing objects, e.g. Using(comparer), are also available.

Describes the possible expectations for Uri. Expectation Negated Summary IsAbsolute IsNotAbsolute an absolute URI IsFile IsNotFile a file URI IsLoopback IsNotLoopback references the local host IsUnc IsNotUnc a UNC path HasDefaultPort DoesNotHaveDefaultPort uses the default port of its scheme HasPort use HasPort().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected port HasScheme use HasScheme().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected scheme HasHost use HasHost().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected host HasPath use HasPath().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected path HasFragment use HasFragment().NotEqualTo(…) has the expected fragment IsBaseOf IsNotBaseOf a base URI of the expected URI HasQueryParameter DoesNotHaveQueryParameter has a query parameter, optionally with a value

You can verify what kind of URI the Uri is, or that it is not: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(uri).IsAbsolute(); await That(uri).IsNotFile(); await That(uri).IsNotLoopback(); await That(uri).IsNotUnc(); For example, a relative URI is not absolute, so Uri uri = new("/tracks/1", UriKind.Relative); await That(uri).IsAbsolute(); fails with: Failure message Expected that uri is an absolute URI, but it was /tracks/1

You can verify that the Uri uses the default port of its scheme, or that it does not: await That(new Uri("https://music.example.com/tracks/1")).HasDefaultPort(); await That(new Uri("https://music.example.com:8443/tracks/1")).DoesNotHaveDefaultPort();

You can verify the port of the Uri. Without an explicit port, it is the default port of the scheme: Uri uri = new("https://localhost:5001/health"); await That(uri).HasPort().EqualTo(5001); await That(uri).HasPort().Between(5000).And(5999); await That(new Uri("http://localhost:4000/health")).HasPort(4000);

You can verify the scheme of the Uri: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(uri).HasScheme("https"); await That(uri).HasScheme().NotEqualTo("http"); As RFC 3986 defines the scheme as case-insensitive, it is compared ignoring case by default, also without an expected value or with a match type. Add .IgnoringCase(false) to compare it case-sensitively, which a .Using(comparer) or a match type of your own that cannot ignore the casing needs as well.

You can verify the host of the Uri: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(uri).HasHost("music.example.com"); await That(uri).HasHost("*.example.com").AsWildcard(); await That(uri).HasHost().EndingWith(".example.com"); As RFC 3986 defines the host as case-insensitive, it is compared ignoring case by default, like the scheme.

You can verify the URL-decoded path of the Uri: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks/1"); await That(uri).HasPath("/tracks/1"); await That(uri).HasPath().StartingWith("/tracks/"); await That(new Uri("https://music.example.com/my%20song")).HasPath("/my song"); An encoded slash (%2F) stays encoded, as it is part of a segment and does not separate two segments: await That(new Uri("https://music.example.com/artists/AC%2FDC")).HasPath("/artists/AC%2FDC"); HasScheme, HasHost, HasPath and HasFragment with an expected value support the same string options and match types as comparing strings, e.g. IgnoringCase() or AsWildcard(). Without an expected value, they offer further comparisons on the property. Containing on the scheme, host, path or fragment counts the occurrences like Contains on a string, so it also accepts a quantifier and a match type: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/albums/1/tracks/2"); await That(uri).HasPath().Containing("/").Exactly(4); await That(uri).HasPath().Containing("tr?cks").AsWildcard().Once();

You can verify the URL-decoded fragment of the Uri, without the leading #: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks/1#lyrics"); await That(uri).HasFragment("lyrics"); await That(uri).HasFragment().NotEqualTo("credits");

You can verify that the Uri is a base URI of another absolute URI, or that it is not: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/api/"); await That(uri).IsBaseOf("https://music.example.com/api/tracks/1"); await That(uri).IsNotBaseOf(new Uri("https://other.example.com/api/tracks/1")); warning Like Uri.IsBaseOf, only the part of the Uri up to its last / is considered, so https://music.example.com/api is also a base URI of https://music.example.com/tracks/1.

You can verify that the Uri has a query parameter, optionally with the expected value, or that it does not have it: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks?page=2&genre=Jazz"); await That(uri).HasQueryParameter("page"); await That(uri).HasQueryParameter("page").WithValue("2"); await That(uri).HasQueryParameter("genre").WithValue("jazz").IgnoringCase(); await That(uri).HasQueryParameter("genre").WithValue("J*").AsWildcard(); await That(uri).DoesNotHaveQueryParameter("token"); Names and values are URL-decoded, and names are compared case-sensitively. WithValue supports the same string options and match types as comparing strings and requires the query parameter to occur exactly once. A query parameter that occurs several times can be verified with WithValues, which compares the values in the order in which they appear in the URI, unless InAnyOrder() is specified. It supports the same options as comparing string collections. You can also add expectations on the value or on all values of the query parameter: Uri uri = new("https://music.example.com/tracks?tag=live&tag=remastered"); await That(uri).HasQueryParameter("tag").WithValues("live", "remastered"); await That(uri).HasQueryParameter("tag") .WhoseValues(values => values.Contains("live")); Like WithValue, WhoseValue requires the query parameter to occur exactly once, also when it is negated.
aweXpect.Xml extends aweXpect with expectations for XML strings and System.Xml.Linq.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Xml --prerelease <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Xml" Version="4.0.0-beta.0.pre.3" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Xml" Version="4.0.0-beta.0.pre.3" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Xml" /> Latest version: 4.0.0-beta.0.pre.3 The package brings Expect.That with it, but not the expectations for strings, numbers or collections, so reference aweXpect as well, e.g. for the IsEqualTo of IsEqualTo(…).AsXml(). The expectations live in the namespace aweXpect, so using aweXpect; is all you need. The examples write That(...) instead of Expect.That(...), which needs using static aweXpect.Expect; (see Getting started).

string xml = """<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles" />"""; // verify that a string is a well-formed XML document await That(xml).IsValidXml(); // verify that a string is equal to the expected XML, compared by its content instead of its formatting await That(xml).IsEqualTo("""<track artist="The Beatles" title="Let It Be"></track>""").AsXml(); // verify that an XElement or XDocument contains the expected XML, ignoring additional nodes XElement track = XElement.Parse("""<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles"><genre>rock</genre></track>"""); await That(track).Matches("""<track title="Let It Be"><genre>rock</genre></track>"""); // verify single attributes, child elements and their values await That(track).HasAttribute("artist").EqualTo("The Beatles").And .HasElement("genre", genre => genre.HasValue().EqualTo("rock")); If the element was not closed, i.e. <track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles">, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that xml is valid XML, but it could not be parsed: Unexpected end of file has occurred. The following elements are not closed: track. Line 1, position 47.

Expectations for string: Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo(…).AsXml() IsNotEqualTo(…).AsXml() equal to the expected XML, compared by content IsValidXml IsNotValidXml a well-formed XML document, optionally with expectations on its root IsValidXmlMatching valid XML that matches the expected XML IsValidXmlMatchingExactly valid XML that matches the expected XML exactly Expectations for XElement and XDocument: Expectation Negated Summary Matches matches the expected XML, additional nodes allowed MatchesExactly matches the expected XML exactly HasAttribute DoesNotHaveAttribute has the attribute, optionally with expectations on its value HasAttribute(…).EqualTo(…), … has the attribute, whose value is compared with a string operator, e.g. StartingWith HasElement DoesNotHaveElement has the child element, optionally with expectations on it HasValue the value satisfies the expectations HasValue().EqualTo(…), … the value is compared with a string operator, e.g. EndingWith or Containing(…).AtLeast(2) The comparisons can be relaxed with the options IgnoringAdditionalNodes(), IgnoringElementOrder() and IgnoringMember(path) or IgnoringMembers(path => …), see Matching XML.

XML strings: comparing and validating strings as XML Matching XML: Matches and MatchesExactly, and the options to relax the comparison Attributes and child elements: verifying single attributes, child elements and values

Describes the possible expectations for matching an XElement or an XDocument with an expected XML, and the options to relax the comparison. Expectation Negated Summary Matches matches the expected XML, additional nodes allowed MatchesExactly matches the expected XML exactly

You can verify that an XElement matches an expected XML: XElement track = XElement.Parse("""<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles"><genre>rock</genre></track>"""); await That(track).Matches("""<track title="Let It Be" />"""); await That(track).MatchesExactly(""" <track artist="The Beatles" title="Let It Be"> <genre>rock</genre> </track> """); Matches ignores the attributes and child nodes of the subject that are not in the expected XML, while MatchesExactly fails for them: Matches is MatchesExactly with the option IgnoringAdditionalNodes(). Missing nodes, different values and a different order of the expected child elements fail both, unless you ignore the element order. If the title was "Yesterday" instead, Matches would fail with: Failure message Expected that track matches <track title="Let It Be" />, but it differed as /track/@title was "Yesterday" instead of "Let It Be" XML options: - ignore additional nodes The elements are compared by their content like by AsXml(): attributes regardless of their order, elements and attributes by their namespace and local name instead of their prefix, and without comments and processing instructions. Whitespace-only text between elements is ignored. For an XDocument, its root element is compared: XDocument document = XDocument.Parse("""<?xml version="1.0"?><track title="Let It Be" />"""); await That(document).Matches("""<track title="Let It Be" />"""); You can also verify that an element does not match an expected XML: XElement track = XElement.Parse("""<track title="Let It Be" />"""); await That(track).DoesNotComplyWith(it => it.Matches("""<track title="Yesterday" />""")); Whitespace, paths and documents without a root element Whitespace-only text between elements is ignored also when the subject was loaded with LoadOptions.PreserveWhitespace, unless xml:space="preserve" on the subject or one of its ancestors keeps it. The paths of the differences start at the subject, also when it is nested in a document. A document without a root element fails, also when the expectation is negated.

The options are available wherever XmlOptions are accepted, i.e. Matches, MatchesExactly, IsValidXmlMatching, IsValidXmlMatchingExactly and AsXml(o => …). They work like the options of aweXpect: Option Configures IgnoringAdditionalNodes() ignores additional attributes and child nodes of the subject IgnoringMember(path), IgnoringMembers(path => …) leaves members out of the comparison IgnoringElementOrder() the child elements and texts can be in any order

You can ignore the attributes and child nodes of the subject that are not in the expected XML. The option is available for MatchesExactly, IsValidXmlMatchingExactly and AsXml(), and Matches and IsValidXmlMatching use it by default: string album = """<album id="42" year="1969"><track title="Come Together" /></album>"""; await That(album).IsEqualTo("""<album id="42" />""").AsXml(o => o.IgnoringAdditionalNodes()); The additional nodes are ignored on every level, and the expected nodes are still compared, so that missing nodes, different values and a different order of the expected child elements fail the expectation. The option is listed when the expectation fails: Failure message XML options: - ignore additional nodes With IgnoringAdditionalNodes(false), Matches and IsValidXmlMatching compare exactly, like MatchesExactly and IsValidXmlMatchingExactly.

You can ignore members whose values change between runs, e.g. generated ids or timestamps. The options are available for Matches, MatchesExactly, IsValidXmlMatching, IsValidXmlMatchingExactly and AsXml(): string album = """<album id="42" createdAt="2026-10-17"><track title="Come Together" etag="x1" /></album>"""; await That(album).IsEqualTo("""<album id="1"><track title="Come Together" /></album>""") .AsXml(o => o .IgnoringMember("/album/@id") .IgnoringMember("@createdAt") .IgnoringMembers(path => path.EndsWith("/@etag"))); IgnoringMember matches whole trailing segments of the path: "@createdAt" ignores the attribute on every element and "track/@id" the attribute of every track, while a path starting with /, e.g. "/album/@id", only ignores this member. A segment without a position, e.g. track, matches every element of the name, and track[2] only the second. The names are compared case-sensitively, as in XML. Like the paths, they are local names, so that "track" ignores a track in every namespace, unlike HasElement, which looks up the name with its namespace. IgnoringMembers receives the path of every compared member instead. An ignored attribute, element or text, and everything below it, is neither compared nor reported as missing or unexpected, and an ignored element is not considered for the order of its siblings. The ignored members are listed when the expectation fails: Failure message XML options: - ignore members: ["/album/@id", "@createdAt", path => path.EndsWith("/@etag")] A member to ignore that matched no compared path is named in a failure, with the path it most likely meant, as a misspelled member to ignore would otherwise ignore nothing without notice: Failure message XML options: - ignore members: ["@createdat"] "@createdat" matched no member (did you mean "@createdAt"?) Members that only occur in the subject As additional nodes of the subject are not compared when they are ignored, e.g. by Matches, a member to ignore that only occurs in the subject matches no compared path either, and is named as well, although it is not needed.

By default, the order of the child elements and texts is significant. You can ignore it for all compared elements: XElement album = XElement.Parse(""" """); await That(album).MatchesExactly(""" """, o => o.IgnoringElementOrder()); The texts are paired like the elements, so that the order of the texts in mixed content, e.g.

ac

, is ignored as well. How the children are paired Each expected child is paired with the first unpaired child of the subject with the same name that matches it. The remaining children of the same name are paired in their order, so that their differences are reported, e.g. /album/track[1]/@title was "Here Comes the Sun" instead of "Come Together", and the children that are still unpaired are reported as missing or unexpected. This greedy pairing can fail when additional nodes are ignored, e.g. by Matches, and an expected child matches several children of the subject, even if another pairing would succeed. As the children are no longer paired by their position, a position in a member to ignore, e.g. track[2], refers to the child at this position in each document.

Describes the possible expectations for the attributes, child elements and values of an XElement or an XDocument. Expectation Negated Summary HasAttribute DoesNotHaveAttribute has the attribute, optionally with expectations on its value HasAttribute(…).EqualTo(…), … has the attribute, whose value is compared with a string operator, e.g. StartingWith HasElement DoesNotHaveElement has the child element, optionally with expectations on it HasValue the value satisfies the expectations HasValue().EqualTo(…), … the value is compared with a string operator, e.g. EndingWith or Containing(…).AtLeast(2)

You can verify that an XElement has an attribute, and add expectations on its value with all string expectations of aweXpect: XElement track = XElement.Parse("""<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles" />"""); await That(track) .HasAttribute("title").And .HasAttribute("artist", artist => artist.StartsWith("The")).And .DoesNotHaveAttribute("explicit"); If the artist was "Paul McCartney" instead, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has attribute "title" and has attribute "artist" whose value starts with "The" and does not have attribute "explicit", but value of attribute "artist" was "Paul McCartney", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "Paul McCartney" "The" ↑ (expected prefix) The value can also be compared directly on the result of HasAttribute(name) with the operators of a string property, EqualTo, StartingWith, EndingWith and Containing(…) (each also with Not…), and the string options, e.g. IgnoringCase() or AsWildcard(): await That(track) .HasAttribute("title").EqualTo("let it be").IgnoringCase().And .HasAttribute("artist").StartingWith("The"); If the title was "Yesterday" instead, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has attribute "title" equal to "let it be" ignoring case and has attribute "artist" starting with "The", but value of attribute "title" was "Yesterday", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "Yesterday" "let it be" ↑ (expected) Actual: <track title="Yesterday" artist="The Beatles" /> The expectations on the value are only verified when the attribute exists, otherwise the failure states that the element did not have the attribute, and a negated expectation, e.g. with DoesNotComplyWith, is met. A failed lookup, also a negated one, shows the complete element it ran on as Actual context. Without a title, HasAttribute("title") would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has attribute "title", but it did not have attribute "title" Actual: <track artist="The Beatles" />

You can verify that an element has a child element, and add expectations on it: XElement album = XElement.Parse("""<album><artist><origin city="Liverpool" /></artist></album>"""); await That(album).HasElement("artist", artist => artist .HasElement("origin", origin => origin .HasAttribute("city", city => city.IsEqualTo("Liverpool")))); await That(album).DoesNotHaveElement("bonusTrack"); Only the direct child elements are looked up, and the expectations are verified on the first child element with the name, like by XElement.Element(name). A failed lookup within the expectations on a child element shows this child element, labeled with it, e.g. Actual (element "artist"):, instead of the whole subject. To verify a whole subtree, combine it with Matches: await That(album).HasElement("artist", artist => artist.Matches("""<artist><origin /></artist>""")); To verify all child elements with a name, select them with Whose and use the collection expectations of aweXpect, e.g. the quantifiers with ComplyWith(…): XElement album = XElement.Parse( """ <album title="Abbey Road"> <track title="Come Together" /> <track title="Something" /> <artist name="The Beatles" /> </album> """); await That(album).Whose(a => a.Elements("track"), tracks => tracks.HasCount(2)); await That(album).Whose(a => a.Elements("track"), tracks => tracks .All().ComplyWith(track => track.HasAttribute("title"))); With a third <track title="Here Comes the Sun" />, the first expectation would fail with the following message. As Elements(…) is only enumerated as far as needed, it states a lower bound: Failure message Expected that album whose Elements("track") have exactly 2 items, but Elements("track") had at least 3 items Collection (Elements("track")): [ <track title="Come Together" />, <track title="Something" />, <track title="Here Comes the Sun" />, (… and maybe more) ]

You can add expectations on the value of an element with all string expectations of aweXpect: XElement track = XElement.Parse("""Let It Be"""); await That(track).HasElement("title", title => title.HasValue(value => value.StartsWith("Let"))); If the title was "Yesterday" instead, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has element "title" which has a value which starts with "Let", but value of the element was "Yesterday", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "Yesterday" "Let" ↑ (expected prefix) Like for attributes, the value can also be compared directly on the result of HasValue(): await That(track).HasElement("title", title => title.HasValue().Containing("e").AtLeast(3)); With the title "Let It Be", the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has element "title" which has a value containing "e" at least 3 times, but value of the element contained "e" twice in "Let It Be" Actual (element "title"): Let It Be The value is the concatenated text of all descendant text nodes, including CDATA sections, like XElement.Value. So the value of an element with mixed content, e.g.

axc

, is axc, and the value of an element without text is empty.

All these expectations are also available for an XDocument and apply to its root element: XDocument document = XDocument.Parse("""<album id="42"><artist /></album>"""); await That(document).HasAttribute("id"); await That(document).HasElement("artist", artist => artist.Matches("<artist />")); await That(document).DoesNotHaveElement("bonusTrack"); HasElement looks up a child element of the root element, so HasElement("album") fails for this document, unlike XDocument.Element(name), which returns the root element itself. Documents without a root element A document without a root element fails, also when the expectation is negated: Failure message Expected that document has attribute "id", but it had no root element

Attributes and child elements are looked up by their XName, i.e. by their namespace and local name, but not by their prefix. A child element inherits the default namespace of its parent, so it must be looked up in this namespace: XNamespace music = "urn:music"; XElement album = XElement.Parse("""<album xmlns="urn:music"><track title="Come Together" /></album>"""); await That(album).HasElement(music + "track", track => track.HasAttribute("title")); A name in a namespace is shown as {urn:music}track in the failure message.

Describes the possible expectations for strings that contain XML. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo(…).AsXml() IsNotEqualTo(…).AsXml() equal to the expected XML, compared by content IsValidXml IsNotValidXml a well-formed XML document, optionally with expectations on its root IsValidXmlMatching valid XML that matches the expected XML IsValidXmlMatchingExactly valid XML that matches the expected XML exactly

You can verify that a string is equal to the expected XML, compared by its content instead of its formatting: string album = """"""; string expected = """ """; await That(album).IsEqualTo(expected).AsXml(); If the duration was 259.0 instead, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that album is XML equivalent to , but it differed as /album/track/@durationSeconds was "259.0" instead of "259" Actual: Expected: The documents are equivalent, when they only differ in the order of the attributes, the prefixes of namespaces, as elements and attributes are compared by their namespace and local name, whitespace-only text between elements, unless xml:space="preserve" keeps it, comments, processing instructions and the XML declaration, CDATA sections instead of escaped text, or instead of . Texts and attribute values are compared exactly, including leading and trailing whitespace, and the order of the child elements is significant, unless you ignore the element order. Each difference names the path of the node: every element by its local name, followed by its position among the siblings of the same name, if there are several, e.g. /album/track[2]/@title, and every text as text(). You can ignore members whose values change between runs, e.g. AsXml(o => o.IgnoringMember("@createdAt")), or ignore the additional nodes of the subject to compare it with a part of the XML, e.g. AsXml(o => o.IgnoringAdditionalNodes()). If the subject is not valid XML, the expectation fails with the reason: Failure message Expected that album is XML equivalent to , but it was "", which could not be parsed as XML: Unexpected end of file has occurred. The following elements are not closed: album. Line 1, position 16. Actual: Expected: As XML is compared by its content, AsXml() cannot be combined with IgnoringCase(), Using(comparer) or another match type like AsWildcard(), and it is not available on Contains or DoesNotContain for a string subject. AsXml() is also available on other string comparisons, e.g. on the items of a collection or on the message of an exception: await That(albums).All().AreEqualTo("""""").AsXml(); await That(albums).Contains("""""").AsXml(); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage("""""").AsXml(); The options are available there as well, e.g. to find an item that contains the expected XML: await That(albums).Contains("""""").AsXml(o => o.IgnoringAdditionalNodes()); Pairing of child elements and DTDs The child elements are paired by their path, so an additional element is reported as unexpected instead of shifting the elements after it, and a different order is reported once for their parent. Like for validation, a document type definition (DTD) is prohibited in both strings.

You can verify that a string is a well-formed XML document: string track = """<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles" />"""; await That(track).IsValidXml(); If the closing tag was missing, i.e. <track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles">, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is valid XML, but it could not be parsed: Unexpected end of file has occurred. The following elements are not closed: track. Line 1, position 47. This verifies that the string can be read to its end by an XmlReader without exceptions. The string must contain exactly one root element; a fragment like <a/><b/> or an empty string is not valid XML. The document is not validated against a schema. For security reasons, a document with a document type definition (<!DOCTYPE ...>) is not valid XML: DTD processing is prohibited and external resources are never resolved, so that verifying untrusted input is not exposed to XML external entity (XXE) or entity expansion attacks: Failure message Expected that track is valid XML, but it contained a document type definition (DTD), which is prohibited for security reasons You can add further expectations on the root XElement parsed from the subject: string track = """<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles" />"""; await That(track).IsValidXml(root => root.Matches("""<track title="Let It Be" />""")); The expectations are only verified when the string is valid XML. Or you can verify that the string is valid XML and matches an expected XML in one step: string track = """<track title="Let It Be" artist="The Beatles" />"""; await That(track).IsValidXmlMatching("""<track title="Let It Be" />"""); await That(track).IsValidXmlMatchingExactly("""<track artist="The Beatles" title="Let It Be" />"""); IsValidXmlMatching("""<track title="Yesterday" />""") would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is valid XML which matches <track title="Yesterday" />, but it differed as /track/@title was "Let It Be" instead of "Yesterday" XML options (it): - ignore additional nodes You can also verify that a string is not valid XML: string track = "Let It Be"; await That(track).IsNotValidXml(); If the string is valid XML, e.g. <track title="Let It Be" />, the expectation fails with: Failure message Expected that track is not valid XML, but it was "<track title=\"Let It Be\" />" Parsing, null subjects and negation An encoding in the XML declaration is not checked, as the string is already decoded. Like with XDocument.Parse, whitespace-only text between elements is dropped for the expectations on the root element, unless xml:space="preserve" keeps it. With expectations on the root element and with IsValidXmlMatching or IsValidXmlMatchingExactly, a string that is not valid XML fails also when the expectation is negated, e.g. within DoesNotComplyWith(…), as there is no root element to verify. Only the negation of IsValidXml() without expectations is met by a string that is not valid XML. IsNotValidXml also succeeds for a document with a document type definition, but fails for a null subject like IsValidXml.
.NET Framework 4.8 or .NET 6 or later aweXpect supports test projects on .NET Framework 4.8 and on .NET 6 or later; some features need .NET 8 or later, see target frameworks.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect --prerelease <PackageReference Include="aweXpect" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect" /> Latest version: 4.0.0-pre.3 This documentation describes aweXpect v4, which is available as a pre-release, so the snippets above install the latest pre-release. Without --prerelease or a pre-release version you get v3, which lacks some of the APIs described here. Add the following using directives: the first brings the static Expect class and lots of extension methods into scope, the second lets you write That(...) instead of Expect.That(...): using aweXpect; using static aweXpect.Expect; note The samples in this documentation write durations like 5.Seconds() with the aweXpect.Chronology package, marked with the comment // from the aweXpect.Chronology package; TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5) works as well.

Every expectation starts with That(subject), continues with what you expect and is awaited: MusicLibraryTests.cs using aweXpect; using static aweXpect.Expect; public class MusicLibraryTests { [Test] public async Task Contains_WhenAlbumIsMissing_ShouldReturnFalse() { MusicLibrary sut = new(); bool result = sut.Contains("Unknown Album"); await That(result).IsFalse(); } } That is a member of the static Expect class. With using static aweXpect.Expect;, or a global using static aweXpect.Expect; anywhere in your test project, you can write That(...); without it, write Expect.That(...). All examples in this documentation assume the static using and write That(...). warning An expectation is only evaluated when it is awaited: without await it never fails. The analyzer aweXpect0001 reports a missing await as an error. If it fails, it throws an exception that fails the test with the following message: Failure message Expected that result is False, but it was True

You can add a reason for all expectations that will be included in the exception message: await That(result).IsFalse().Because("the album is not in the library"); The reason then appears in the failure message: Failure message Expected that result is False, because the album is not in the library, but it was True

The expectations are grouped by the type of the subject: What you test Where to look bool, numbers, string, char, enums, Guid, Version, Stream, TimeSpan, DateTime, DateOnly, TimeOnly, any object, equivalency Values IEnumerable<T>, arrays, dictionaries Collections delegates and exceptions, Task, events, callbacks Behavior JSON, XML, HTTP, Uri, IPAddress, reflection, snapshots Extension packages fail, skip or end a test without an expectation: Fail, Skip Test frameworks

How it works explains how expectations are evaluated, negated and combined, how they treat null, the options they share and how to configure their defaults. Setup and integration covers the test frameworks, the target frameworks and Native AOT. Extending aweXpect shows how to add expectations for your own types.

Describes the concepts that all expectations share: how they are built, evaluated, negated, combined, configured and limited in time, and how to change their defaults. How aweXpect fits into your test project, e.g. its test frameworks and target frameworks, is described in setup and integration.
