An expectation that is awaited in an async void method or lambda, e.g. in list.ForEach(async x => await That(x)...), throws its failure after the test has completed, so the test does not observe it. The analyzer aweXpect0005 warns about it. Await the expectation in the test method itself, e.g. in a foreach loop, or return a Task instead.
documents.s: My expectation in a ForEach lambda never fails

documents.t: An expectation starts with That(subject) instead of subject.Should(), the expectations read as Is…, Has… or Contains instead of Be…, Have… or Contain, and the whole expectation is awaited: FluentAssertions title.Should().StartWith("Let").And.EndWith("Be", "it is the last track"); act.Should().Throw<InvalidOperationException>().WithMessage("Yesterday"); aweXpect string title = "Let It Be"; Action act = () => throw new InvalidOperationException("Yesterday"); await That(title).StartsWith("Let").And.EndsWith("Be").Because("it is the last track"); await That(act).Throws<InvalidOperationException>().WithMessage("Yesterday"); .Should().Be(x) becomes IsEqualTo(x), and BeTrue() becomes IsTrue(). The Getting started page lists where to find the expectations for each subject. The because parameter becomes .Because(reason), appended to the expectation it belongs to. .And combines expectations on the same subject as in FluentAssertions, and .Or requires only one of them, see combining expectations. Instead of an AssertionScope, Expect.ThatAll combines expectations on different subjects and reports all failures together.
documents.s: How does the syntax differ from FluentAssertions?

documents.t: Yes. The aweXpect.Migration package reports every FluentAssertions and xUnit assertion, and its code fix rewrites it to aweXpect where it knows an equivalent. A second step with the code fix of aweXpect0001 adds the missing await. The rewrites are listed on Migrating from FluentAssertions. warning aweXpect is strict by default, so some rewritten expectations fail where FluentAssertions passed, e.g. WithMessage compares the whole message unless you add .AsWildcard(). The behavioral differences list these cases.
documents.s: Can I migrate my FluentAssertions tests automatically?

documents.t: This documentation describes aweXpect v4, which is available as a pre-release. Without a pre-release version you get v3, which lacks some of the APIs described here. Getting started shows how to install the pre-release. When you upgrade from v3, some expectations were renamed without an [Obsolete] forwarder, so their old names no longer compile. What's new in v4 lists the renames.

From v4 on, aweXpect, aweXpect.Core, aweXpect.Json, aweXpect.Web, aweXpect.Xml, aweXpect.Reflection and the aweXpect.Snapshots packages are released together with one version. Use the same version for all of them, see one version for all packages.
documents.s: Which versions of the extension packages do I need?

documents.t: That is a member of the static Expect class. Add using static aweXpect.Expect;, or a global using static aweXpect.Expect; anywhere in your test project, or write Expect.That(...), see Getting started.
documents.s: The name That does not exist in the current context

documents.t: The samples in this documentation write durations like 5.Seconds() with the aweXpect.Chronology package. Install it, or write TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5) instead.

Some overloads of aweXpect rely on [OverloadResolutionPriority], which only takes effect with C# 13 or later. C# 13 is the default language version only from .NET 9 on, so a test project with an older language version, e.g. on .NET 8 where C# 12 is the default, can fail with CS0121 in these cases: An async lambda or a lambda that only throws, passed to That(...), fits both the Task and the ValueTask overload, see Delegates. A collection expectation with a string as single item, a params list or a collection expression […] can bind to a different overload or be ambiguous, see Collections. Task PlayAsync() => Task.CompletedTask; await That(async () => await PlayAsync()).DoesNotThrow(); // CS0121 with C# 12 on .NET 8 await That(() => PlayAsync()).DoesNotThrow(); // binds to the Task overload Set the language version to 13 or later in the test project: <PropertyGroup> <LangVersion>13</LangVersion> </PropertyGroup> For a delegate, you can also return the task directly, as in the second line above, or declare a local function and pass it. In aweXpect.Json v4, IsValidJson(null) without a parameter name is ambiguous as well; write IsValidJson(options: null), see What's new in v4.
TUnit declares a Skip class of its own in the TUnit.Core namespace. Where the compiler reports the name as ambiguous, write aweXpect.Skip, see skipping a test.

After an expectation like IsNotNull(), aweXpect suppresses the nullability warnings for the subject, but only for a local variable or a parameter that is checked in a preceding statement of the same method, see the nullability suppressor. For a property or another expression, use the result of the expectation instead, which is not nullable: Track track = new() { Title = "Let It Be" }; string title = await That(track.Title).IsNotNull(); int length = title.Length;

MSTest 3 and 4, NUnit 3, 4 and 5, TUnit, and xUnit v2 and v3. The aweXpect package generates an adapter for them into the test project, so you don't have to configure anything. Another test framework needs an adapter of its own, see test frameworks.
documents.s: Which test frameworks does aweXpect support?

documents.t: A failed expectation throws the assertion exception of the test framework when the test project references the assembly that declares it. Otherwise it throws aweXpect.FailException, which fails the test as well, e.g.: in a TUnit project that only references TUnit.Core and not TUnit.Assertions, in an xUnit v2 project that only references xunit.core and not xunit.assert, in a test project on .NET 8 or later that sets <LangVersion> below 9, where the generated adapter cannot register itself, see aweXpect2002. The thrown exception for each test framework is listed under failed expectations.
documents.s: A failure throws aweXpect.FailException instead of the exception of my test framework

documents.t: xUnit v2 cannot skip a running test, so Skip.Test, Skip.When and Skip.Unless fail it instead, and Fail.Inconclusive fails it as well, as xUnit v2 has no inconclusive outcome. When no test framework is detected, as described above, aweXpect throws its own aweXpect.SkipException or aweXpect.InconclusiveException, and the outcome depends on the runner. The outcome for each test framework is listed under skipping a test and inconclusive.
documents.s: A skipped test is reported as failed

documents.t: Describes the possible expectations for single values, from bool and numbers to strings, streams and any object. Page Expectations Boolean IsTrue, IsFalse, Implies Number IsEqualTo, IsGreaterThan, IsBetween, IsPositive, IsNaN, Within String IsEqualTo with wildcards or regex, StartsWith, Contains, HasLength Char IsEqualTo, categories like IsALetter or IsWhiteSpace Enum IsEqualTo, HasValue, IsDefined, HasFlag Guid IsEqualTo, IsEmpty, IsNullOrEmpty Version IsEqualTo, IsGreaterThan, IsBetween, HasMajor Stream IsReadable, IsSeekable, HasLength, HasPosition TimeSpan IsEqualTo, IsGreaterThan, IsBetween, IsPositive, Within DateTime / DateTimeOffset IsEqualTo, IsAfter, IsBefore, IsBetween, HasYear, Within DateOnly / TimeOnly IsEqualTo, IsAfter, IsBefore, IsBetween, HasYear Exception HasMessage, HasParamName, HasHResult, HasInner, HasRecursiveInnerExceptions Object IsEqualTo, IsSameAs, Is<T>, IsNull, Satisfies, CompliesWith, IsCollected Equivalency IsEquivalentTo and its options A few rules apply to all of these pages: The object expectations, such as IsNull, IsSameAs, Is<T>, Satisfies, CompliesWith or IsEquivalentTo, work on every subject, also on the types of the other pages. A null subject fails every expectation that inspects it, and its negation as well, as the rule for null subjects describes. The Has… expectations, such as HasLength() or HasYear(), continue with a comparison like GreaterThan or Between, as shown for the length of a string. They have no negated twin, so the overview tables list "negated comparison" for them: negate the comparison instead, e.g. HasLength().NotEqualTo(3). The options page lists the options that several expectations share, e.g. a tolerance with Within or the string options.

Describes the possible expectations for bool and bool? values. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected value IsTrue IsNotTrue (only bool?) true IsFalse IsNotFalse (only bool?) false IsNull IsNotNull (only bool?) null Implies DoesNotImply false, or the other value is true
You can verify that the bool is equal to another one or not: bool isPlayed = false; await That(isPlayed).IsEqualTo(false); await That(isPlayed).IsNotEqualTo(true);

You can verify that the bool is true or false: await That(false).IsFalse(); await That(true).IsTrue(); Awaiting a bool without any expectation is a shorthand for IsTrue(): bool isInLibrary = true; await That(isInLibrary); The negations and the null checks are only available for a bool?: bool? isPlayed = null; await That(isPlayed).IsNotFalse() .Because("it could be true or null"); await That(isPlayed).IsNotTrue() .Because("it could be false or null"); await That(isPlayed).IsNull(); note On a bool?, IsNotTrue() and IsNotFalse() succeed for null.
You can verify that a implies b or not: bool isPlayed = false; bool isInLibrary = true; await That(isPlayed).Implies(isInLibrary); await That(isInLibrary).DoesNotImply(isPlayed);

Describes the possible expectations for char values. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected character IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected characters IsAnAsciiLetter IsNotAnAsciiLetter an ASCII letter IsAnAsciiDigit IsNotAnAsciiDigit an ASCII digit IsAnAsciiHexDigit IsNotAnAsciiHexDigit an ASCII hexadecimal digit IsALetter IsNotALetter a Unicode letter IsADigit IsNotADigit a decimal digit IsANumber IsNotANumber a Unicode number IsUpperCased IsNotUpperCased an upper-case letter IsLowerCased IsNotLowerCased a lower-case letter IsAControlCharacter IsNotAControlCharacter a control character IsWhiteSpace IsNotWhiteSpace whitespace .NET 8 or later On .NET 8 or later char is an INumber<char>, so the ordering expectations, IsBetween, IsPositive and IsNegative of the number expectations also accept a char. Below .NET 8 they are not available for char.

You can verify that the char is equal to another one or not: char initial = 'a'; await That(initial).IsEqualTo('a'); await That(initial).IsNotEqualTo('b'); await That(initial).IsEqualTo('A').IgnoringCase();

You can verify that the char is one of many alternatives: char initial = 'a'; await That(initial).IsOneOf('a', 'b', 'c'); await That(initial).IsNotOneOf('x', 'y', 'z'); await That(initial).IsOneOf('A', 'B', 'C').IgnoringCase();

You can verify the category of the char, or that it does not belong to it: await That('a').IsAnAsciiLetter(); await That('乐').IsALetter(); await That('3').IsADigit(); await That('½').IsANumber().And.IsNotADigit(); await That('A').IsUpperCased(); await That('\t').IsWhiteSpace().And.IsAControlCharacter(); await That(' ').IsNotAControlCharacter(); Each expectation follows the corresponding method of char: Expectation Method IsAnAsciiLetter char.IsAsciiLetter IsAnAsciiDigit char.IsAsciiDigit IsAnAsciiHexDigit char.IsAsciiHexDigit IsALetter char.IsLetter IsADigit char.IsDigit IsANumber char.IsNumber IsUpperCased char.IsUpper IsLowerCased char.IsLower IsAControlCharacter char.IsControl IsWhiteSpace char.IsWhiteSpace IsADigit only accepts decimal digits, while IsANumber also accepts characters like '½'. Casing of a char vs. a string IsUpperCased and IsLowerCased differ from the string casing expectations, which only look at cased letters: '1' is neither upper-cased nor lower-cased, while "1" is both. IgnoringCase() compares the characters the same way as strings with IgnoringCase(), i.e. with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase.

Describes the possible expectations for DateOnly and TimeOnly. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected value IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected values IsAfter IsNotAfter later than the expected value IsOnOrAfter IsNotOnOrAfter not earlier than the expected value IsBefore IsNotBefore earlier than the expected value IsOnOrBefore IsNotOnOrBefore not later than the expected value IsBetween IsNotBetween between two values, both bounds included HasYear, … negated comparison has the expected year, month, day, hour, … .NET 8 or later The DateOnly and TimeOnly expectations are only available on .NET 8 or later.

You can verify that the DateOnly or TimeOnly is equal to another one or not: DateOnly TimeOnly DateOnly releaseDate = new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsEqualTo(new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotEqualTo(new DateOnly(1970, 5, 8)); TimeOnly startTime = new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16); await That(startTime).IsEqualTo(new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16)); await That(startTime).IsNotEqualTo(new TimeOnly(13, 15, 16));

You can verify that the DateOnly or TimeOnly is one of many alternatives: DateOnly TimeOnly DateOnly releaseDate = new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsOneOf([new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26), new DateOnly(1970, 5, 8)]); await That(releaseDate).IsNotOneOf([new DateOnly(1965, 8, 6), new DateOnly(1966, 8, 5)]); TimeOnly startTime = new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16); await That(startTime).IsOneOf([new TimeOnly(14, 15, 15), new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16)]); await That(startTime).IsNotOneOf([new TimeOnly(13, 15, 16), new TimeOnly(13, 14, 15)]);

You can verify that the DateOnly or TimeOnly is (on or) after or before another value, or that it is not: DateOnly TimeOnly DateOnly releaseDate = new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsAfter(new DateOnly(1968, 11, 22)); await That(releaseDate).IsOnOrAfter(new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26)); await That(releaseDate).IsBefore(new DateOnly(1970, 5, 8)); await That(releaseDate).IsOnOrBefore(new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotAfter(new DateOnly(1970, 5, 8)); TimeOnly startTime = new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16); await That(startTime).IsAfter(new TimeOnly(12, 0)); await That(startTime).IsOnOrAfter(new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16)); await That(startTime).IsBefore(new TimeOnly(18, 0)); await That(startTime).IsOnOrBefore(new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16)); await That(startTime).IsNotAfter(new TimeOnly(18, 0));

You can verify that the DateOnly or TimeOnly is between two values, or that it is not: DateOnly TimeOnly DateOnly releaseDate = new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsBetween(new DateOnly(1969, 1, 1)).And(new DateOnly(1969, 12, 31)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotBetween(new DateOnly(1970, 1, 1)).And(new DateOnly(1970, 12, 31)); TimeOnly startTime = new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16); await That(startTime).IsBetween(new TimeOnly(14, 0)).And(new TimeOnly(15, 0)); await That(startTime).IsNotBetween(new TimeOnly(18, 0)).And(new TimeOnly(20, 0)); Both bounds are included. For a TimeOnly, a maximum below the minimum runs across midnight, see clock face.

Every comparison on this page except the Has… properties accepts a tolerance with Within, which widens the accepted range by the tolerance: DateOnly TimeOnly DateOnly releaseDate = new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsEqualTo(new DateOnly(1969, 9, 25)).Within(TimeSpan.FromDays(1)) .Because("we accept values between 1969-09-24 and 1969-09-26"); await That(releaseDate).IsBefore(new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26)).Within(TimeSpan.FromDays(1)); TimeOnly startTime = new TimeOnly(14, 15, 16); await That(startTime).IsEqualTo(new TimeOnly(14, 15, 17)).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)) .Because("we accept values between 14:15:16 and 14:15:18"); await That(startTime).IsOneOf([new TimeOnly(14, 15, 17)]).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); Tolerance for a DateOnly A DateOnly tolerance is a whole number of days. Of the default tolerance only the whole days apply, so a default below one day has no effect on a DateOnly.

A TimeOnly has no date, so midnight is not a boundary for equality and ranges, but it stays one for ordering: IsEqualTo, IsNotEqualTo and IsOneOf use the shortest distance around the clock face, so 00:00 and 23:59 are one minute apart. IsBetween runs clockwise from the minimum to the maximum, so a range from 23:00 to 01:00 contains 00:00. IsAfter, IsOnOrAfter, IsBefore and IsOnOrBefore compare the times as they are, so 00:00 is never after 23:00. TimeOnly midnight = new TimeOnly(0, 0); await That(midnight).IsBetween(new TimeOnly(23, 0)).And(new TimeOnly(1, 0)); await That(midnight).IsEqualTo(new TimeOnly(23, 59)).Within(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)); await That(midnight).IsNotAfter(new TimeOnly(23, 0)); Tolerance around midnight The distance around the clock face never exceeds 12 hours, so a tolerance of 12 hours or more accepts every time in IsEqualTo and IsOneOf. The tolerance of IsAfter, IsOnOrAfter, IsBefore and IsOnOrBefore only ever widens the accepted range and never wraps around midnight.

You can verify the properties of the DateOnly or TimeOnly: DateOnly TimeOnly DateOnly releaseDate = new DateOnly(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).HasYear(1969); await That(releaseDate).HasMonth().GreaterThan(6); await That(releaseDate).HasDay(26); await That(releaseDate).HasDayOfWeek(DayOfWeek.Friday); TimeOnly startTime = new TimeOnly(15, 16, 17, 189); await That(startTime).HasHour(15); await That(startTime).HasMinute(16); await That(startTime).HasSecond().LessThan(30); await That(startTime).HasMillisecond(189); The Has… expectations whose value is a number or a TimeSpan, e.g. HasLength(), HasCount(), HasYear() or HasMajor(), continue with one of the following comparisons, each with a negated counterpart: Comparison Negated Succeeds when the value is EqualTo(x) NotEqualTo(x) equal to x GreaterThan(x) NotGreaterThan(x) greater than x GreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) NotGreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) greater than or equal to x LessThan(x) NotLessThan(x) less than x LessThanOrEqualTo(x) NotLessThanOrEqualTo(x) less than or equal to x Between(min).And(max) NotBetween(min).And(max) between min and max, both bounds included Passing the value directly, e.g. HasYear(1969), is a shorthand for EqualTo. Comparing with null The expected value is nullable, e.g. to pass a value mapped from a property. As the actual value is never null, EqualTo(null) fails and NotEqualTo(null) succeeds, while a comparison of order against null, such as GreaterThan(null) or Between(null).And(3), fails even when negated. HasDayOfWeek only offers EqualTo and NotEqualTo.

Describes the possible expectations for DateTime and DateTimeOffset. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected value IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected values IsAfter IsNotAfter later than the expected value IsOnOrAfter IsNotOnOrAfter not earlier than the expected value IsBefore IsNotBefore earlier than the expected value IsOnOrBefore IsNotOnOrBefore not later than the expected value IsBetween IsNotBetween between two values, both bounds included HasYear, … negated comparison has the expected year, month, day, hour, … HasDayOfWeek negated comparison falls on the expected day of the week HasKind negated comparison a DateTime with the expected Kind HasOffset negated comparison a DateTimeOffset with the expected Offset

You can verify that the DateTime or DateTimeOffset is equal to another one or not: DateTime DateTimeOffset DateTime releaseDate = new DateTime(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsEqualTo(new DateTime(1969, 9, 26)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotEqualTo(new DateTime(1970, 5, 8)); using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package DateTimeOffset releaseDate = new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()); await That(releaseDate).IsEqualTo(new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())); await That(releaseDate).IsNotEqualTo(new DateTimeOffset(1970, 5, 8, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()));

You can verify that the DateTime or DateTimeOffset is one of many alternatives: DateTime DateTimeOffset DateTime releaseDate = new DateTime(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsOneOf([new DateTime(1969, 9, 26), new DateTime(1970, 5, 8)]); await That(releaseDate).IsNotOneOf([new DateTime(1965, 8, 6), new DateTime(1966, 8, 5)]); using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package DateTimeOffset releaseDate = new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()); await That(releaseDate).IsOneOf([ new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()), new DateTimeOffset(1970, 5, 8, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())]); await That(releaseDate).IsNotOneOf([ new DateTimeOffset(1965, 8, 6, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()), new DateTimeOffset(1966, 8, 5, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())]);

You can verify that the DateTime or DateTimeOffset is (on or) after or before another value, or that it is not: DateTime DateTimeOffset DateTime releaseDate = new DateTime(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsAfter(new DateTime(1968, 11, 22)); await That(releaseDate).IsOnOrAfter(new DateTime(1969, 9, 26)); await That(releaseDate).IsBefore(new DateTime(1970, 5, 8)); await That(releaseDate).IsOnOrBefore(new DateTime(1969, 9, 26)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotAfter(new DateTime(1970, 5, 8)); using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package DateTimeOffset releaseDate = new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()); await That(releaseDate).IsAfter(new DateTimeOffset(1968, 11, 22, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())); await That(releaseDate).IsOnOrAfter(new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())); await That(releaseDate).IsBefore(new DateTimeOffset(1970, 5, 8, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())); await That(releaseDate).IsOnOrBefore(new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours())); await That(releaseDate).IsNotAfter(new DateTimeOffset(1970, 5, 8, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()));

You can verify that the DateTime or DateTimeOffset is between two values, or that it is not: DateTime DateTimeOffset DateTime releaseDate = new DateTime(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsBetween(new DateTime(1969, 1, 1)).And(new DateTime(1969, 12, 31)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotBetween(new DateTime(1970, 1, 1)).And(new DateTime(1970, 12, 31)); using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package DateTimeOffset releaseDate = new DateTimeOffset(1969, 9, 26, 10, 0, 0, 1.Hours()); await That(releaseDate) .IsBetween(new DateTimeOffset(1969, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1.Hours())) .And(new DateTimeOffset(1969, 12, 31, 23, 59, 59, 1.Hours())); await That(releaseDate) .IsNotBetween(new DateTimeOffset(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1.Hours())) .And(new DateTimeOffset(1970, 12, 31, 23, 59, 59, 1.Hours())); Both bounds are included.

Every comparison on this page except the Has… properties accepts a tolerance with Within, which widens the accepted range by the tolerance, the same way for DateTime and DateTimeOffset: DateTime importedAt = DateTime.Now; await That(importedAt).IsEqualTo(DateTime.Now).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)) .Because("the import should have taken less than one second"); await That(importedAt).IsOneOf([DateTime.Now]).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); await That(importedAt).IsAfter(DateTime.Now).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); await That(importedAt).IsOnOrBefore(DateTime.Now).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); await That(importedAt).IsBetween(DateTime.Today).And(DateTime.Now).Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); Without Within, the default tolerance applies, if one is configured.

aweXpect refuses to compare a DateTime with DateTimeKind.Utc against one with DateTimeKind.Local, because they describe different instants: every comparison fails, except IsNotEqualTo and IsNotOneOf. A value with DateTimeKind.Unspecified is compatible with both kinds, and a DateTimeOffset is always comparable: DateTime releaseDate = new DateTime(1969, 9, 26, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc); // fails with "but it had kind Utc, which cannot be compared with Local" await That(releaseDate).IsBefore(new DateTime(1969, 9, 27, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Local)); await That(releaseDate).IsNotEqualTo(new DateTime(1969, 9, 26, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Local)); await That(releaseDate).IsEqualTo(new DateTime(1969, 9, 26, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Unspecified)); The same rule applies wherever a DateTime is compared as a value, e.g. in collection expectations and in IsEquivalentTo. Details of the Kind rule The negated ordering expectations IsNotAfter, IsNotBefore, IsNotOnOrAfter, IsNotOnOrBefore and IsNotBetween fail for an incompatible pair as well. For IsBetween and IsNotBetween the subject must be comparable to both bounds. For IsOneOf and IsNotOneOf an alternative with an incompatible Kind can never be the match, but the remaining alternatives are still considered. In a collection, two values that differ only in their kind never match: DateTime[] releaseDates = [new DateTime(1969, 9, 26, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Utc)]; // fails, because the expected value denotes a different instant await That(releaseDates).Contains(new DateTime(1969, 9, 26, 0, 0, 0, DateTimeKind.Local));

You can verify the properties of DateTime or DateTimeOffset: DateTime importedAt = new DateTime(2024, 12, 31, 15, 16, 17, 189, DateTimeKind.Utc); // or: DateTimeOffset importedAt = new(2024, 12, 31, 15, 16, 17, 189, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(90)); await That(importedAt).HasYear(2024); await That(importedAt).HasMonth(12); await That(importedAt).HasDay(31); await That(importedAt).HasHour().GreaterThan(12); await That(importedAt).HasMinute(16); await That(importedAt).HasSecond(17); await That(importedAt).HasMillisecond().LessThan(500); await That(importedAt).HasDayOfWeek(DayOfWeek.Tuesday); await That(importedAt).HasDayOfWeek().NotEqualTo(DayOfWeek.Sunday); For DateTime you can also verify the Kind property, and for DateTimeOffset the Offset property: DateTime DateTimeOffset DateTime importedAt = new DateTime(2024, 12, 31, 15, 16, 17, 189, DateTimeKind.Utc); await That(importedAt).HasKind(DateTimeKind.Utc); await That(importedAt).HasKind().NotEqualTo(DateTimeKind.Local); DateTimeOffset importedAt = new DateTimeOffset(2024, 12, 31, 15, 16, 17, 189, TimeSpan.FromMinutes(90)); await That(importedAt).HasOffset(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(90)); await That(importedAt).HasOffset().GreaterThan(TimeSpan.Zero); The Has… expectations whose value is a number or a TimeSpan, e.g. HasLength(), HasCount(), HasYear() or HasMajor(), continue with one of the following comparisons, each with a negated counterpart: Comparison Negated Succeeds when the value is EqualTo(x) NotEqualTo(x) equal to x GreaterThan(x) NotGreaterThan(x) greater than x GreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) NotGreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) greater than or equal to x LessThan(x) NotLessThan(x) less than x LessThanOrEqualTo(x) NotLessThanOrEqualTo(x) less than or equal to x Between(min).And(max) NotBetween(min).And(max) between min and max, both bounds included Passing the value directly, e.g. HasYear(2024), is a shorthand for EqualTo. Comparing with null The expected value is nullable, e.g. to pass a value mapped from a property. As the actual value is never null, EqualTo(null) fails and NotEqualTo(null) succeeds, while a comparison of order against null, such as GreaterThan(null) or Between(null).And(3), fails even when negated. HasDayOfWeek and HasKind only offer EqualTo and NotEqualTo.

Describes the possible expectations for enum values. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected value IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected values HasValue negated comparison has the expected underlying numeric value IsDefined IsNotDefined a named member or combination of flags HasFlag DoesNotHaveFlag has the expected flag set The samples on this page use the following enum: enum Genre { Rock = 1, Pop = 2, Jazz = 3, Blues = 4 }
You can verify that the enum is equal to another one or not: await That(Genre.Rock).IsEqualTo(Genre.Rock); await That(Genre.Rock).IsNotEqualTo(Genre.Jazz);
You can verify that the enum is one of many alternatives: await That(Genre.Rock).IsOneOf(Genre.Rock, Genre.Pop, Genre.Jazz); await That(Genre.Blues).IsNotOneOf(Genre.Rock, Genre.Pop, Genre.Jazz);

You can verify that the enum has a given underlying numeric value or not: await That(Genre.Rock).HasValue(1); await That(Genre.Rock).HasValue().NotEqualTo(2); await That(Genre.Jazz).HasValue().GreaterThan(2); The Has… expectations whose value is a number or a TimeSpan, e.g. HasLength(), HasCount(), HasYear() or HasMajor(), continue with one of the following comparisons, each with a negated counterpart: Comparison Negated Succeeds when the value is EqualTo(x) NotEqualTo(x) equal to x GreaterThan(x) NotGreaterThan(x) greater than x GreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) NotGreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) greater than or equal to x LessThan(x) NotLessThan(x) less than x LessThanOrEqualTo(x) NotLessThanOrEqualTo(x) less than or equal to x Between(min).And(max) NotBetween(min).And(max) between min and max, both bounds included Passing the value directly, e.g. HasValue(1), is a shorthand for EqualTo. Comparing with null The expected value is nullable, e.g. to pass a value mapped from a property. As the actual value is never null, EqualTo(null) fails and NotEqualTo(null) succeeds, while a comparison of order against null, such as GreaterThan(null) or Between(null).And(3), fails even when negated.

You can verify that the enum has a defined value or not: await That((Genre)3).IsDefined() .Because("3 corresponds to 'Jazz'"); await That((Genre)5).IsNotDefined() .Because("5 is no valid genre"); For an enum with the [Flags] attribute, a combination of the bits of its named members is defined as well, while a value with any other bit set is not: using System.Text.RegularExpressions; await That(RegexOptions.Multiline | RegexOptions.IgnoreCase).IsDefined(); await That((RegexOptions)(1 << 20)).IsNotDefined(); Zero is only defined if a member names it, like RegexOptions.None does.

You can verify that the enum has a specific flag or not: using System.Text.RegularExpressions; RegexOptions options = RegexOptions.Multiline | RegexOptions.IgnoreCase; await That(options).HasFlag(RegexOptions.IgnoreCase); await That(options).DoesNotHaveFlag(RegexOptions.ExplicitCapture);

Describes how to verify that two objects are equivalent (that is, structurally equal) rather than referentially or strictly equal. Equivalency walks both objects recursively and compares them member by member. Expectation Negated Summary IsEquivalentTo IsNotEquivalentTo structurally equal to the expected object AreEquivalentTo use None() the selected items are equivalent to the expected value Equivalent() switches an equality expectation to equivalency Equality (IsEqualTo) delegates to object.Equals, which for most reference types means reference equality. Equivalency instead compares the public state of two objects field by field and property by property, recursing into nested objects and collections. Two objects are equivalent when every included member compares as equivalent. When you publish with trimming or Native AOT, see Native AOT and trimming.

You can verify that any object is equivalent to an expected object with IsEquivalentTo, or that it is not with IsNotEquivalentTo. Both accept an optional callback to configure the comparison via EquivalencyOptions<TExpected>: using aweXpect.Equivalency; // for the options, e.g. `IgnoringMember` await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected); await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o.IgnoringMember("PlayCount")); await That(album).IsNotEquivalentTo(unexpected);

You can verify that the selected items of an IEnumerable<T> (or IAsyncEnumerable<T>) are equivalent to a single expected value with AreEquivalentTo, using the same equivalency comparison: IEnumerable<Track> tracks = //... Track expected = //... await That(tracks).All().AreEquivalentTo(expected); await That(tracks).AtLeast(2).AreEquivalentTo(expected, o => o.IgnoringMember("Title")); The equivalency options go into AreEquivalentTo itself. To compare the items with a custom comparer, use AreEqualTo(expected).Using(comparer).

For expectations that accept a custom equality comparer (IsEqualTo, Contains, StartsWith, EndsWith, HasItem, All().AreEqualTo(...), …), append .Equivalent() to switch the comparison from Equals to structural equivalency: await That(album).IsEqualTo(expected).Equivalent(); IEnumerable<Track> tracks = //... Track expectedTrack = //... await That(tracks).Contains(expectedTrack).Equivalent(); await That(tracks).StartsWith(expectedTrack).Equivalent(); await That(tracks).All().AreEqualTo(expectedTrack).Equivalent(o => o.IgnoringCollectionOrder()); Like IsEquivalentTo, a failure lists the equivalency options that were used.

Equivalency takes the public fields and properties of the expected object and compares each one with the member of the same name on the actual object, recursing into nested objects. How a value is compared depends on its type: Type Compared primitives, enum, string, decimal, DateTime, DateTimeOffset, DateOnly, TimeOnly, TimeSpan, Guid, BigInteger, Complex, Half, NFloat, Int128, UInt128 by value, with Equals MemberInfo (and therefore Type), Assembly, Module, Delegate, Uri, CultureInfo, IPAddress, Encoding and anything derived from them by value, with Equals Task, Task<T> and anything derived from them by reference, without waiting for a result ValueTask, ValueTask<T> by value, with Equals StringBuilder by its text, so it also matches a string JsonElement, JsonNode by its compact JSON text Regex by its pattern and options collections (IEnumerable<T>), Memory<T>, ReadOnlyMemory<T> item by item, in order sets (ISet<T>, IReadOnlySet<T>) item by item, without an order dictionaries (IDictionary, IDictionary<TKey, TValue>, IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TValue>) entry by entry, by key everything else by its members, recursively

Only the members of the expected object are compared; additional members of the actual object are ignored. A member that the actual object doesn't have is reported as missing instead of being compared against null. A field and a property of the same name match each other, so a class with public fields can be compared against an anonymous object, which only has properties. Fields, properties and explicitly implemented interface properties When a field and a property of the same name match, the same kind is preferred, and only included kinds are considered: with IncludingFields(IncludeMembers.None) an expected property no longer matches a field. An expected member that the actual object doesn't have is also matched against a property that the actual type implements explicitly for an interface (int IHasId.Id => 1;), by its short name. A public field or property of that name always takes precedence, and a name that the actual type implements explicitly for more than one interface is reported as ambiguous. Failures name the kind of the expected member.

As soon as either side is compared by value, both are: a string is only equivalent to an equal string, and swapping subject and expectation doesn't change the result. A type that is compared by members ignores its own Equals, also when it implements IEqualityComparer, so an Equals can neither hide differing members nor reject matching ones. To let Equals decide, compare the type by value; to check a member against your own criterion, use It.Is<T>(). A JsonElement or JsonNode is compared by its JSON text without the whitespace between tokens, so the order of the properties and the notation of numbers still matter: {"a":1.0} differs from {"a":1}.

A set on either side is enough to match the items without an order, exactly like ignoring collection order, so a HashSet<T> can be compared against an array. A multi-dimensional array is only equivalent to an array of the same rank with the same length in every dimension, as for IsEqualTo. A dictionary reports a differing, missing or superfluous entry under its key. A collection or dictionary type that declares members itself is compared by its items or entries and, in addition, by these members, so two pages with the same items but a different TotalCount are not equivalent. They are compared like the members of any other object: they come from the expected type, so against an array, which declares none, only the items count, and the options apply to them. // class Playlist : List<Track> { public string Name { get; set; } } await That(playlist).IsEquivalentTo(expectedPlaylist); // compares the tracks only await That(playlist).IsEquivalentTo(expectedPlaylist, o => o.IgnoringMember("Name")); Which members of a collection type are compared The members that describe the collection are left out, because the items already cover them: members that a type of the framework declares, which is a type in the System or Microsoft namespaces, e.g. the Count and Capacity of a List<T> or the Comparer, Keys and Values of a Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, also when your type overrides them, properties that implement a property of an interface of the framework, e.g. the Count of an IReadOnlyCollection<T> or the Keys of an IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TValue> that your type implements itself, what the compiler generates, e.g. the state of an iterator method. Every other public field or property is compared, whether your type or one of its base types declares it, including one that hides a member of the framework with new. This also holds for the collection types of other libraries: to leave a member out, ignore it, where a For<T> registration limits the rule to the collection type, or compare the type by value to let its Equals decide. Sets and dictionaries with a custom comparer An actual set that was created with a custom comparer, e.g. a HashSet<T> or a SortedSet<T>, uses that comparer to decide which items are the same. Each expected key is looked up through the actual dictionary, so its key comparer decides which keys are the same, as it does for IsEqualTo. An expected item that the comparer of the actual set finds in it is matched, whatever its members are, and only the remaining items are matched by the equivalency comparison. This also holds for an ImmutableHashSet<T>, an ImmutableSortedSet<T> and a FrozenSet<T> on .NET 8 or later. A sorted set considers two items the same when its comparer orders neither before the other. The comparer of an expected set is not used. The key comparer is read from the same dictionaries as for IsEqualTo. Two expected keys that it considers the same can't both be matched by one entry, so the second one is reported as lacking a distinct key. In a project that enables trimming or Native AOT, the comparer of a set or a dictionary is only read for the types that the source generator sees.

Cyclic references are detected, so graphs that reference themselves don't recurse forever. An instance that is referenced more than once is still compared against each of its expected counterparts. The comparison fails at a recursion depth of 100 nested objects instead of overflowing the stack, see Limiting the recursion depth. A type without any members to compare throws an InvalidOperationException instead of succeeding without verifying anything. Include the relevant members, compare the type by value, or exclude all members explicitly with IncludeMembers.None. The same instance on both sides The same instance on both sides is equivalent to itself, unless its type is compared by value: its members, entries or items are not read, so a shared singleton without members (e.g. EventArgs.Empty) does not throw.

All equivalency overloads accept an options callback that receives an EquivalencyOptions (or EquivalencyOptions<TExpected>) record. The fluent methods are chainable: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .IncludingFields() .IgnoringMember("PlayCount") .IgnoringCollectionOrder()); Option Effect IgnoringMember ignores members by name IgnoringMembers, IgnoringFields, IgnoringProperties ignores members by path and type IncludingFields, IncludingProperties chooses which fields and properties are compared IgnoringCollectionOrder matches collection items without an order Comparing<TActual, TExpected> compares a pair of types with a predicate Mapping compares differently named members For<T> applies options to members of type T only ComparisonType compares a type by value or by its members LimitingRecursionDepth changes the maximum recursion depth of 100

await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o.IgnoringMember("PlayCount")); The match is case-insensitive. For nested members, the path is dot-separated (e.g. "Artist.Name"); for collection items, the index is bracketed (e.g. "Tracks[3]"), and for dictionary entries the key, formatted with the invariant culture (e.g. "Ratings[4.5]"). The name must cover whole segments at the end of the member path, so "Name" ignores every member called Name at any depth, while "ame" or "t.Name" ignore nothing.

The number of lambda parameters tells what the predicate matches: one parameter receives the member path, two parameters receive the member path and type: // by member path and type await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .IgnoringMembers((memberPath, memberType) => memberPath.EndsWith("PlayCount") && memberType == typeof(int))); // by member path only await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .IgnoringMembers(memberPath => memberPath == "Artist.Name")); // by type only await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .IgnoringMembers((_, memberType) => memberType == typeof(DateTime))); Use IgnoringFields or IgnoringProperties instead of IgnoringMembers to restrict a predicate to one kind of member. They take the same member path and type, and are never applied to collection items, which are neither a field nor a property: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .IgnoringProperties((memberPath, _) => memberPath.EndsWith("PlayCount"))); Which type is passed to the predicate A field or property is matched by its declared type, with Nullable<T> unwrapped, so the last IgnoringMembers example also ignores a DateTime? member, but not an object member that holds a DateTime. A collection item or a dictionary value is matched by the runtime type of its value, or by object when it is null.

You can change which fields and properties participate in the comparison. Both methods accept an IncludeMembers flags enum with the values None, Public and Internal: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .IncludingFields(IncludeMembers.None) // exclude all fields .IncludingProperties(IncludeMembers.Public | IncludeMembers.Internal)); Default for both is IncludeMembers.Public. IncludeMembers.Internal also includes protected internal members, because the whole assembly can access them. Other protected and private members are never compared, because they are implementation details of a type. To compare such a type, let its Equals decide by comparing it by value.

When comparing collections, order matters by default. To disable that: int[] subject = [1, 2, 3]; int[] expected = [3, 2, 1]; await That(subject).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o.IgnoringCollectionOrder()); Pass false to re-enable ordered comparison if it was disabled globally. The items do not have to be comparable: each expected item is matched against an item that is equivalent to it, and every element can be matched only once, so [1, 1, 2] is not equivalent to [1, 2, 2]. When no such matching covers both collections, only the items that were left over are reported, each against the leftover item it differs from the least.

When the actual and the expected objects have different types whose members don't correspond by name, e.g. your tracks and the entries of a chart, let a predicate decide whether a pair is equivalent: await That(tracks).IsEquivalentTo(chart, o => o .Comparing<Track, ChartEntry>((track, entry) => track.Title == entry.Song) .IgnoringCollectionOrder()); The predicate applies wherever an actual TActual meets an expected TExpected, at any depth and also for derived types, and decides instead of the comparison by value or by members. A pair that doesn't match is reported with its path and the predicate: Failure message Expected that tracks is equivalent to chart, but it was not: Element [1] did not match (track, entry) => track.Title == entry.Song: Actual: Track { IsPlayed = True, PlayCount = 42, Title = "Midnight Echo" } Expected: ChartEntry { Plays = 42, Song = "Neon Skyline" } Equivalency options: - include public fields and properties - compare Track with ChartEntry by (track, entry) => track.Title == entry.Song When a predicate applies A null value is never passed to the predicate. When several predicates apply to a pair, the one that was added last decides. Within For<T>, a predicate only applies to values of type T and to the values nested in them.
documents.s: Comparing different types with a predicate

documents.t: When the members of both types correspond but are named differently, map them, so that they are still compared member by member and a failure names the exact difference: await That(tracks).IsEquivalentTo(chart, o => o .Mapping<Track, ChartEntry>(track => track.Title, entry => entry.Song) .Mapping<Track, ChartEntry>(track => track.PlayCount, entry => entry.Plays)); The mapping applies wherever an actual TActual meets an expected TExpected. Failures and members to ignore name the expected member, e.g. Property Song differed. Without the types, a mapping matches the expected member by name, like IgnoringMember, at any depth: await That(tracks).IsEquivalentTo(chart, o => o .Mapping("Title", "Song") .Mapping("PlayCount", "Plays")); Either member can be nested, so a mapping also flattens an object, e.g. the artist of a release: // class ReleaseDto { public string ArtistName { get; set; } } // class Release { public Artist Artist { get; set; } } await That(releaseDto).IsEquivalentTo(release, o => o .Mapping<ReleaseDto, Release>(dto => dto.ArtistName, release => release.Artist.Name)); How mappings are applied The expressions are only read for the names of their members, so they also work with trimming or Native AOT. A null value on the way to the actual member reads as null. A null value on the way to the expected member, for which the actual object has no member, makes each mapped actual member below it compare with null. When the actual object has no member for an expected member that a mapping runs through, like Artist above, every member below it has to be mapped as well. The others are reported as missing, so nothing is left unverified. When the actual object has such a member, it is compared as usual, and only the mapped member below it reads another member. A mapping by name reads the actual member on the actual object that is compared with the object which has the first member of the expected path, so Mapping("ArtistName", "Artist.Name") flattens like the example above, and Mapping("Artist.Alias", "Artist.Name") reads the alias of the actual artist. When several mappings apply to an expected member, the one that was added last decides. A mapping by name that matched no member is named below it in the failure, like a member to ignore.

You can apply options to a specific member type only. Type-specific options override the top-level options for members of that type or of a derived type. When several registrations match, the most derived one wins: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .For<Artist>(x => x.IgnoringMember("BornOn")) .For<List<Track>>(x => x.IgnoringCollectionOrder())); How registrations are applied For<T> throws an ArgumentException for an interface; register the implementing class or struct instead. Like the other fluent methods, For<T> returns a copy and leaves the options it was called on unchanged. The callback is applied to the final options of the expectation, so every other option applies to T as well, no matter whether it is set before or after For<T>. A registration in the callback of a single expectation replaces one for the same type in the customized default. The options are looked up by the runtime type of a value, which is never an interface. A registration for a nullable value type T? applies to T, because a boxed value cannot tell the two apart, so it also applies to members of type T. When the subject and the expectation have different types and both are registered, the registration for the type of the expectation wins, because the members that are compared come from the expectation. An extension can read the options that apply to a type with GetOptionsFor(type).

Each type is compared either by value (Equals decides alone) or by its members (Equals is ignored). The default depends on the type (see Default behavior). One side compared by value is enough. Comparing by value is how you ask for the equality a type defines for itself, e.g. a value object that compares only its Id. To override for a specific type: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o .For<TrackId>(x => x with { ComparisonType = EquivalencyComparisonType.ByValue })); To change the global rule, replace the DefaultComparisonTypeSelector: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o with { DefaultComparisonTypeSelector = type => type == typeof(TrackId) ? EquivalencyComparisonType.ByValue : EquivalencyDefaults.DefaultComparisonType(type), }); Which comparison type a member uses Unlike the other type-specific options, the comparison type applies to the type itself and not to its members: a member without a registration of its own falls back to the comparison type of the top-level options or, if none is set, to the DefaultComparisonTypeSelector, so a string member of a type compared by members is still compared by value. When only the expectation is compared by value, the expectation's Equals decides.
documents.s: Comparing by value or by members

documents.t: Equivalency walks nested objects recursively, so a graph that is deep enough would overflow the stack and take the whole test process with it. The comparison therefore stops after 100 nested objects on a single path and reports the member path at which the limit was hit (shown here with the limit lowered to 3): Failure message Expected that subject is equivalent to expected, but it was not: Property Next.Next.Next exceeded the maximum recursion depth of 3 Equivalency options: - include public fields and properties - limit the recursion depth to 3 Use LimitingRecursionDepth to raise or lower the limit: await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(expected, o => o.LimitingRecursionDepth(500)); It is equivalent to setting MaxRecursionDepth directly. A limit other than the default is listed in the failure message under Equivalency options:. How the depth is counted The depth is counted per path, so two members on the same level are both at the same depth, and members that are compared by value do not add to it. A cyclic reference is caught by the cycle detection and never reaches the limit.

You can change the default EquivalencyOptions via the configuration. Every equivalency expectation starts from them: they are used as they are when no callback is provided, and a callback receives them as its starting point: using aweXpect.Customization; using IDisposable scope = Customize.aweXpect.Equivalency().DefaultEquivalencyOptions .Set(new EquivalencyOptions().IgnoringCollectionOrder()); // All equivalency checks within this scope ignore collection order by default. To change the default for all async flows, e.g. in an assembly-level setup, set it on Customize.aweXpect.Global: using aweXpect.Customization; Customize.aweXpect.Global.Equivalency().DefaultEquivalencyOptions .Set(new EquivalencyOptions().IgnoringCollectionOrder());

Equivalency lets you compare against an anonymous expectation object in which individual members assert their own expectations via It.Is<T>(). Think of it as a playlist filter: each property carries its own criterion rather than a concrete value: class Track { public string? Title { get; set; } public int PlayCount { get; set; } } Track midnight = new() { Title = "Midnight Echo", PlayCount = 42, }; await That(midnight).IsEquivalentTo(new { Title = It.Is<string>().That.IsNotEmpty(), PlayCount = It.Is<int>().That.IsGreaterThan(2), }); It.Is<T>() (without .That) only asserts that the property has the given type. Properties that are null The type of null cannot be determined, so for a null property the expectations are verified against null when T is a reference type or a nullable value type: It.Is<string>().That.IsNull() succeeds, while e.g. It.Is<string>().That.IsEmpty() fails. For a non-nullable value type T, such as int, a null property always fails.

Failure messages list each differing member with its full path and the configured options used for the comparison. For a structural mismatch: Failure message Expected that album is equivalent to expected, but it was not: Property Artist.Name differed: Actual: "Wings" Expected: "The Beatles" Equivalency options: - include public fields and properties When the playlist-filter pattern with It.Is<T>() fails, e.g. for a track with PlayCount = 1, the member's expectation is rendered as Expected: Failure message Expected that midnight is equivalent to new { Title = It.Is<string>().That.IsNotEmpty(), PlayCount = It.Is<int>().That.IsGreaterThan(2), }, but it was not: Property PlayCount differed: Actual: 1 Expected: is int that is greater than 2 Equivalency options: - include public fields and properties

Describes the possible expectations for Guid values. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected value IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected values IsEmpty IsNotEmpty Guid.Empty IsNullOrEmpty IsNotNullOrEmpty null or Guid.Empty (only Guid?)

You can verify that the Guid is equal to another one or not: Guid albumId = Guid.Parse("5c01d9d2-66f7-4782-8c14-e54eae9aaacc"); await That(albumId).IsEqualTo(Guid.Parse("5c01d9d2-66f7-4782-8c14-e54eae9aaacc")); await That(albumId).IsNotEqualTo(Guid.Parse("cdd7a485-40a1-4bba-bb8b-d0e903704b02"));

You can verify that the Guid is one of many alternatives: Guid albumId = Guid.Parse("5c01d9d2-66f7-4782-8c14-e54eae9aaacc"); await That(albumId).IsOneOf( Guid.Parse("5c01d9d2-66f7-4782-8c14-e54eae9aaacc"), Guid.Parse("cdd7a485-40a1-4bba-bb8b-d0e903704b02")); await That(albumId).IsNotOneOf( Guid.Parse("cdd7a485-40a1-4bba-bb8b-d0e903704b02"), Guid.Parse("f1a0a5f4-1f63-4dd4-8d42-6d2f7a0a1c11"));

You can verify that the Guid is (null or) empty or not: await That(Guid.Empty).IsEmpty(); await That(Guid.NewGuid()).IsNotEmpty(); Guid? missingId = Guid.Empty; await That(missingId).IsNullOrEmpty(); Guid? albumId = Guid.NewGuid(); await That(albumId).IsNotNullOrEmpty();

Describes the possible expectations for numbers. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected number IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected numbers IsGreaterThan IsNotGreaterThan greater than the expected number IsGreaterThanOrEqualTo IsNotGreaterThanOrEqualTo greater than or equal to the expected number IsLessThan IsNotLessThan less than the expected number IsLessThanOrEqualTo IsNotLessThanOrEqualTo less than or equal to the expected number IsBetween IsNotBetween between two numbers, both bounds included IsPositive IsNotPositive greater than zero IsNegative IsNotNegative less than zero IsNaN IsNotNaN NaN (floating point numbers only) IsFinite IsNotFinite neither infinite nor NaN (floating point numbers only) IsInfinite IsNotInfinite positive or negative infinity (floating point numbers only) .NET 8 or later Below .NET 8 these expectations only accept byte, sbyte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float, double and decimal, and IsPositive and IsNegative only the signed ones of them. On .NET 8 or later they also accept other INumber<T> types, e.g. char, nint, Half, Int128 or BigInteger.
You can verify that the number is equal to another one or not: int playCount = 42; await That(playCount).IsEqualTo(42); await That(playCount).IsNotEqualTo(41);
You can verify that the number is one of many alternatives: int trackCount = 12; await That(trackCount).IsOneOf(10, 12, 14); await That(trackCount).IsNotOneOf(11, 13);

You can verify that the number is greater than or less than (or equal to) another number, or that it is not: int playCount = 42; await That(playCount).IsGreaterThan(41); await That(playCount).IsGreaterThanOrEqualTo(42); await That(playCount).IsLessThan(43); await That(playCount).IsLessThanOrEqualTo(42); await That(playCount).IsNotGreaterThan(42); await That(playCount).IsNotLessThan(42);

You can verify that the number is between two numbers: int playCount = 42; await That(playCount).IsBetween(41).And(43); await That(playCount).IsNotBetween(43).And(50); Both bounds belong to the range, so IsNotBetween(42).And(50) fails for 42.

You can verify that the number is positive or negative, or that it is not: await That(42).IsPositive(); await That(-3).IsNegative(); await That(0).IsNotPositive(); await That(0).IsNotNegative(); Zero and NaN are neither positive nor negative, so both IsNotPositive and IsNotNegative succeed for them.

For floating point numbers you can verify that the number is NaN, finite or infinite, or that it is not: await That(float.NaN).IsNaN(); await That(42.0).IsNotNaN(); await That(42.0).IsFinite(); await That(float.PositiveInfinity).IsInfinite(); await That(double.NaN).IsNotFinite().And.IsNotInfinite(); NaN is neither greater nor less than any number, so it satisfies IsNotGreaterThan(5) although it fails IsLessThanOrEqualTo(5).

The comparisons on this page, except the sign, NaN and infinity checks, accept a tolerance with Within, which widens the accepted range by the tolerance: double duration = 42.1; await That(duration).IsEqualTo(42).Within(0.2) .Because("we accept values between 41.8 and 42.2 (42 ± 0.2)"); await That(duration).IsOneOf(40, 42, 44).Within(0.2) .Because("we accept values between 39.8 and 40.2 or 41.8 and 42.2 or 43.8 and 44.2"); await That(duration).IsGreaterThan(42.2).Within(0.2) .Because("we accept values greater than 42.0 (42.2 - 0.2)"); await That(duration).IsLessThan(42).Within(0.2) .Because("we accept values less than 42.2 (42 + 0.2)"); For double, float, decimal and Half, Percent() directly after Within interprets the tolerance as a percentage of the expected value, or of each bound: double durationSeconds = 1040.0; await That(durationSeconds).IsEqualTo(1000).Within(5).Percent() .Because("we accept values between 950 and 1050 (1000 ± 5%)"); await That(durationSeconds).IsBetween(1000).And(2000).Within(5).Percent() .Because("we accept values between 950 and 2100"); The percentage is taken of the absolute value, so IsEqualTo(-1000).Within(5).Percent() accepts values between -1050 and -950. An expected value of zero only accepts zero.

Describes the possible expectations for any object. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected object IsSameAs IsNotSameAs the same reference as the expected object IsEquatableTo IsNotEquatableTo equal according to its IEquatable<T> implementation IsEquivalentTo IsNotEquivalentTo structurally equal to the expected object IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected objects Is<T> IsNot<T> of type T or a derived type IsExactly<T> IsNotExactly<T> exactly of type T IsNull IsNotNull null Satisfies DoesNotSatisfy satisfies a predicate CompliesWith DoesNotComplyWith meets a nested expectation Whose a member meets a nested expectation IsCollected IsNotCollected the target of a WeakReference is garbage collected

You can verify that the object is equal to another one or not: record Album(string Title); Album album = new("Abbey Road"); await That(album).IsEqualTo(new Album("Abbey Road")); await That(album).IsNotEqualTo(new Album("Revolver")); This uses the object.Equals(object?, object?) method. Numbers typed as object A number typed as object also equals a number of another numeric type with the same value (e.g. 1 and 1L) in equality (IsEqualTo, IsOneOf, Contains, ContainsValue), but not in equivalency. For Half, Int128 and UInt128 this only applies on .NET 8 or later.

You can verify that the object has the same reference as another one: record Album(string Title); Album album = new("Abbey Road"); await That(album).IsSameAs(album); await That(album).IsNotSameAs(new Album("Abbey Road")); This uses the object.ReferenceEquals(object?, object?) method.

You can verify that the object is equal to another one while using a custom IEqualityComparer<object>: class AlbumComparer : IEqualityComparer<object> { public bool Equals(object? x, object? y) => (x as Album)?.Title == (y as Album)?.Title; public int GetHashCode(object obj) => obj.GetHashCode(); } Album album = new("Abbey Road"); await That(album).IsEqualTo(new Album("Abbey Road")).Using(new AlbumComparer());

You can verify that the object is equal to a value by using its IEquatable<T> implementation, also when the value has a different type: class TrackId(long value) : IEquatable<long> { public bool Equals(long other) => value == other; } TrackId trackId = new(42); await That(trackId).IsEquatableTo(42L); await That(trackId).IsNotEquatableTo(7L);

You can verify that the object is structurally equivalent to another one. See the equivalency page for details and configuration options: Album album = new("Abbey Road"); await That(album).IsEquivalentTo(new Album("Abbey Road")); await That(album).IsNotEquivalentTo(new Album("Revolver")); Use IsEqualTo when the type defines what equal means, e.g. a record or a type that overrides Equals. Use IsEquivalentTo when it does not, e.g. for a class that only has reference equality, or when some members should be ignored. .Equivalent() switches an expectation that compares with Equals, e.g. Contains or All().AreEqualTo on a collection, to the same equivalency.

You can verify that the object is one of many alternatives: record Album(string Title); Album album = new("Abbey Road"); await That(album).IsOneOf([new Album("Abbey Road"), new Album("Revolver")]); await That(album).IsNotOneOf([new Album("Revolver"), new Album("Help!")]);

You can verify that the object is of a given type or a derived type, or that it is not: object album = new Album("Abbey Road"); await That(album).Is<Album>(); await That(album).Is(typeof(Album)); await That(album).IsNot<Track>(); await That(album).IsNot(typeof(Track)); IsExactly and IsNotExactly do not accept a derived type: object album = new Album("Abbey Road"); await That(album).IsExactly<Album>(); await That(album).IsExactly(typeof(Album)); await That(album).IsNotExactly<Track>(); await That(album).IsNotExactly(typeof(Track));
You can verify that the object is null or not: object? album = null; await That(album).IsNull(); await That(new Album("Abbey Road")).IsNotNull();

You can verify that any object satisfies a given predicate: Track track = new() { Title = "Let It Be", PlayCount = 3 }; await That(track).Satisfies(x => x.PlayCount > 0); await That(track).DoesNotSatisfy(x => x.IsPlayed); When the object changes in the background, Within(…) waits until it satisfies the predicate, see waiting for a condition.

You can verify that any object complies with an expectation: List<Track> tracks = new(); await That(tracks).CompliesWith(x => x.IsEmpty()); await That(tracks).DoesNotComplyWith(x => x.HasCount().GreaterThan(0)); DoesNotComplyWith succeeds when the nested expectation fails. Like Satisfies, CompliesWith can wait for the object with Within(…). Which one to use: Satisfies for a quick check with a predicate; a failure only shows the predicate and the object. CompliesWith to reuse other expectations, e.g. IsEmpty() or a string option; a failure explains what the nested expectation found. Whose to verify a member of the object; a failure names the member and its value.

You can verify that the target of a WeakReference or WeakReference<T> is garbage collected or not: using System.Runtime.CompilerServices; WeakReference released = CreateReleasedReference(); Album album = new("Let It Be"); WeakReference<Album> cached = new(album); await That(released).IsCollected(); await That(cached).IsNotCollected() .Because("the album is still in use"); GC.KeepAlive(album); [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.NoInlining)] static WeakReference CreateReleasedReference() => new(new Album("Abbey Road")); A reference held by the test keeps the target alive A strong reference that the test itself still holds keeps the target alive, e.g. a local variable or the temporary object in new WeakReference(new Album(…)), which a Debug build keeps until the end of the method, even when it is no longer used. The example above therefore creates the released album in a separate method. For an object the test creates itself, use IsCollectedAfter instead, which creates the object where no reference to it remains. How the garbage collection is triggered Both force full blocking garbage collections before they check the target, and repeat them a few times, as finalizers can release further objects.

Describes the possible expectations for Stream and BufferedStream. Expectation Negated Summary IsReadable IsNotReadable supports reading IsWritable IsNotWritable supports writing IsSeekable IsNotSeekable supports seeking IsReadOnly IsNotReadOnly supports reading, but not writing IsWriteOnly IsNotWriteOnly supports writing, but not reading HasLength negated comparison has the expected length in bytes HasPosition negated comparison is at the expected position HasBufferSize negated comparison a BufferedStream with the expected buffer size

You can verify what the Stream supports, or that it does not support it: using Stream playlist = new MemoryStream(); await That(playlist).IsReadable(); await That(playlist).IsSeekable(); await That(playlist).IsWritable(); await That(playlist).IsNotReadOnly(); using FileStream album = File.Open("album.txt", FileMode.OpenOrCreate, FileAccess.Read); await That(album).IsReadOnly() .Because("the file was opened with Read access"); using FileStream log = File.Open("album.log", FileMode.OpenOrCreate, FileAccess.Write); await That(log).IsWriteOnly() .Because("the file was opened with Write access");

You can verify the length of the Stream: using Stream playlist = new MemoryStream("Help"u8.ToArray()); await That(playlist).HasLength(4); await That(playlist).HasLength().Between(3).And(5); The Has… expectations whose value is a number or a TimeSpan, e.g. HasLength(), HasCount(), HasYear() or HasMajor(), continue with one of the following comparisons, each with a negated counterpart: Comparison Negated Succeeds when the value is EqualTo(x) NotEqualTo(x) equal to x GreaterThan(x) NotGreaterThan(x) greater than x GreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) NotGreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) greater than or equal to x LessThan(x) NotLessThan(x) less than x LessThanOrEqualTo(x) NotLessThanOrEqualTo(x) less than or equal to x Between(min).And(max) NotBetween(min).And(max) between min and max, both bounds included Passing the value directly, e.g. HasLength(3), is a shorthand for EqualTo. Comparing with null The expected value is nullable, e.g. to pass a value mapped from a property. As the actual value is never null, EqualTo(null) fails and NotEqualTo(null) succeeds, while a comparison of order against null, such as GreaterThan(null) or Between(null).And(3), fails even when negated.

You can verify the position of the Stream: using Stream playlist = new MemoryStream("Help"u8.ToArray()); playlist.Seek(2, SeekOrigin.Current); await That(playlist).HasPosition(2); await That(playlist).HasPosition().GreaterThan(1);

.NET 8 or later The buffer size expectations are only available on .NET 8 or later. You can verify the buffer size of the BufferedStream: using BufferedStream playlist = new(new MemoryStream("Help"u8.ToArray()), 2); await That(playlist).HasBufferSize(2); await That(playlist).HasBufferSize().NotEqualTo(3);

Describes the possible expectations for strings. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo equal to the expected string, or matching a pattern IsOneOf IsNotOneOf equal to one of the expected strings IsNull IsNotNull null IsEmpty IsNotEmpty the empty string IsNullOrEmpty IsNotNullOrEmpty null or the empty string IsNullOrWhiteSpace IsNotNullOrWhiteSpace null, empty or only whitespace HasLength negated comparison has the expected number of characters HasLineCount negated comparison has the expected number of lines HasLines its lines meet collection expectations StartsWith DoesNotStartWith starts with the expected string EndsWith DoesNotEndWith ends with the expected string Contains DoesNotContain contains the expected substring, optionally a number of times IsUpperCased IsNotUpperCased every letter with an upper-case form is upper-case IsLowerCased IsNotLowerCased every letter with a lower-case form is lower-case IsParsableInto<T> IsNotParsableInto<T> can be parsed into T

You can verify that the string is equal to another one or not: string title = "Abbey Road"; await That(title).IsEqualTo("Abbey Road"); await That(title).IsNotEqualTo("Let It Be"); The comparison is ordinal and can be configured with the string options or compare against a pattern. The failure message points at the first difference. When multi-line values differ in several places, a Differences context lists the changed lines with their line numbers in the actual and the expected value. Each difference is surrounded by one unchanged line, and differences that are close together are shown as one block: Failure message Differences: 2 2 host = localhost - 3 port = 8080 + 3 port = 8081 4 4 timeout = 30 5 5 [client] 6 6 retries = 3 - 7 verbose = true - 8 log = file + 7 log = console Tabs and other invisible characters are shown as escape sequences. Which differences are listed Lines that only differ in what the string options ignore are not listed. At most MaximumNumberOfCollectionItems differences are listed (see formatting). With a custom comparer (Using(…)), which compares whole values, no differences are listed.

The expectations that compare the string with an expected string (IsEqualTo, IsOneOf, StartsWith, EndsWith, Contains and their negations) take the following options: Option Effect IgnoringCase() compares with StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase IgnoringNewlineStyle() treats 
, 
 and  as equal IgnoringIndentation() removes the leading whitespace from every line (see below) IgnoringLeadingWhiteSpace() ignores whitespace at the start of the strings IgnoringTrailingWhiteSpace() ignores whitespace at the end of the strings NormalizingWhiteSpace() collapses whitespace runs to a space and trims (see below) AsBlock() matches an indented block of lines (see below) Using(comparer) compares with a custom IEqualityComparer<string> string title = "Abbey Road"; await That(title).IsEqualTo("ABBEY ROAD").IgnoringCase(); await That("Abbey
Road").IsEqualTo("Abbey
Road").IgnoringNewlineStyle(); await That(" Abbey
 Road").IsEqualTo("Abbey
Road").IgnoringIndentation(); await That(title).IsEqualTo(" Abbey Road").IgnoringLeadingWhiteSpace(); await That(title).IsEqualTo("Abbey Road 	").IgnoringTrailingWhiteSpace(); await That("Abbey
	 Road ").IsEqualTo("Abbey Road").NormalizingWhiteSpace(); await That(title).StartsWith("ABBEY").Using(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase); The same options apply wherever strings are compared, e.g. to the items of a collection of strings or to the message of an exception. The negations take the same options, so an option can make them fail: string title = "Abbey Road"; await That(title).DoesNotEndWith("ROAD") .Because("the casing differs, which would not count with `IgnoringCase()`"); Whitespace at the inner end and ignoring the case with Using The whitespace options only ignore whitespace at the start or the end of the subject. A prefix, suffix or substring keeps the whitespace at its inner end, unless that end reaches the corresponding end of the subject: await That("Abbey").StartsWith("Abbey ").IgnoringTrailingWhiteSpace(); await That("AbbeyRoad").DoesNotStartWith("Abbey ").IgnoringTrailingWhiteSpace(); To ignore the case with Using(…), pass a case-insensitive comparer such as StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase instead of adding IgnoringCase().

While IgnoringLeadingWhiteSpace only trims the start of the complete string, IgnoringIndentation removes the leading whitespace from every line. This allows comparing against a raw string literal that is indented differently than the subject: string code = """ public class Beatles { public string Album => "Abbey Road"; } """; await That(code).Contains(""" public string Album => "Abbey Road"; """).IgnoringIndentation(); This also normalizes the newline style. Trailing whitespace within a line is kept, but a line that consists only of whitespace becomes empty.

NormalizingWhiteSpace replaces every run of whitespace, including line breaks and tabs, with a single space and removes the whitespace at the start and the end. This compares generated SQL, HTML or log output regardless of its layout: string sql = """ SELECT * FROM Albums WHERE Title = 'Abbey Road' """; await That(sql).IsEqualTo("SELECT * FROM Albums WHERE Title = 'Abbey Road'").NormalizingWhiteSpace(); await That(sql).Contains("FROM Albums WHERE").NormalizingWhiteSpace(); await That("AbbeyRoad").IsNotEqualTo("Abbey Road").NormalizingWhiteSpace(); Whitespace is collapsed, not removed, so "AbbeyRoad" still differs from "Abbey Road". Any Unicode whitespace counts, e.g. also a non-breaking space. Combining NormalizingWhiteSpace with other options It makes IgnoringIndentation, IgnoringNewlineStyle, IgnoringLeadingWhiteSpace and IgnoringTrailingWhiteSpace redundant, as it removes every difference that they ignore. They can still be specified. It applies to the patterns of AsWildcard and AsRegex as well, so a regex sees a single space where the subject had a line break. As the line breaks of the pattern are collapsed too, a comment in a pattern with RegexOptions.IgnorePatternWhitespace extends to the end of the pattern. Like with the other whitespace options, a prefix, suffix or substring keeps the whitespace at its inner end, which then has to match whitespace in the subject, unless that end reaches the corresponding end of the subject. It cannot be combined with AsBlock, which compares the lines that the normalization joins. A failure shows the values with normalized whitespace and the position of the first difference refers to them. Where the failure shows the normalized subject, the original one is listed below it. No differences per line are listed.

While IgnoringIndentation removes the leading whitespace from every line, AsBlock keeps the relative indentation within the expected block and only allows the block as a whole to be indented in the subject. This is stricter, as a line that is indented differently from the rest of the block does not match: string code = """ public class Beatles { public string Album { get; } } """; await That(code).Contains(""" public string Album { get; } """).AsBlock(); The block must start and end at line boundaries, and all its lines must share the same whitespace prefix in the subject. AsBlock also works with IsEqualTo, where the whole text has to be the block, e.g. for an XML element that keeps the indentation of the document it was taken from, and with the expectations on a collection of strings, such as HasItem: string album = """ <album> <title>Abbey Road</title> <length>47:03</length> </album> """; await That(album).IsEqualTo(""" <album> <title>Abbey Road</title> <length>47:03</length> </album> """).AsBlock(); Whitespace lines, newlines and other options in a block A line that consists only of whitespace matches any line that consists only of whitespace. The newline style is always ignored, and a single trailing line terminator does not start a new line, so "a
b
" has the same two lines as "a
b" (as for lines). AsBlock can be combined with IgnoringCase, Using and the count quantifiers; the whitespace, newline and indentation options throw an InvalidOperationException after it.

Instead of comparing for equality, IsEqualTo can match the subject against a pattern, a prefix or a suffix. The same match types are available for IsNotEqualTo, IsOneOf and IsNotOneOf. Contains and DoesNotContain search within the subject, so they take a pattern, but no prefix or suffix: use StartsWith or EndsWith for that.

string title = "Let It Be"; await That(title).IsEqualTo("Let*B?").AsWildcard(); Wildcard specifier Matches * (asterisk) Zero or more characters ? (question mark) Exactly one character (a surrogate pair counts as one) The pattern has to cover the complete subject, including all its lines and a trailing newline.

string title = "Let It Be"; await That(title).IsEqualTo("(.*)Be").AsRegex(); Unlike a wildcard, the pattern may match any part of the subject: IsEqualTo("It").AsRegex() succeeds for "Let It Be". Enclose the pattern in \A and \z to match the complete subject. IgnoringCase() adds RegexOptions.IgnoreCase and RegexOptions.CultureInvariant. Every other option is opt-in: using System.Text.RegularExpressions; string lyrics = "Come together\nRight now"; await That(lyrics).IsEqualTo("^Right now$").AsRegex(RegexOptions.Multiline);

string title = "Abbey Road"; await That(title).IsEqualTo("Abbey").AsPrefix(); await That(title).IsEqualTo("Road").AsSuffix(); Regex engine, timeout and corner cases A wildcard or regex pattern is matched by the regex engine, which can't use a custom comparer, so combining Using(…) with AsWildcard() or AsRegex() throws an InvalidOperationException. Matching a pattern is limited to the DefaultRegexTimeout, one second by default. A pattern that takes longer, e.g. because of catastrophic backtracking, throws an ArgumentException that names the timeout and asks you to simplify the pattern. In a regex, ^ and $ bind to the start and the end of the subject and not to every line, but $ also matches before a trailing newline. The regex engine applies its own case folding, which can differ from the other expectations for a few characters, e.g. the Kelvin sign (U+212A) on modern .NET.

You can verify that the string is one of many alternatives, with the same options as for equality: string title = "Abbey Road"; await That(title).IsOneOf("Help!", "Abbey Road", "Revolver"); await That(title).IsOneOf("HELP!", "ABBEY ROAD", "REVOLVER").IgnoringCase(); await That(title).IsNotOneOf("Help!", "Revolver");

You can verify that the string is null, empty or contains only whitespace: string? title = null; await That(title).IsNull(); await That("Abbey Road").IsNotNull(); await That("").IsEmpty(); await That("Abbey Road").IsNotEmpty(); await That(title).IsNullOrEmpty(); await That("Abbey Road").IsNotNullOrEmpty(); await That(title).IsNullOrWhiteSpace(); await That("Abbey Road").IsNotNullOrWhiteSpace();

You can verify that the string has the expected length: string title = "Abbey Road"; await That(title).HasLength(10); await That(title).HasLength().Between(8).And(12); await That(title).HasLength().NotGreaterThan(12); The Has… expectations whose value is a number or a TimeSpan, e.g. HasLength(), HasCount(), HasYear() or HasMajor(), continue with one of the following comparisons, each with a negated counterpart: Comparison Negated Succeeds when the value is EqualTo(x) NotEqualTo(x) equal to x GreaterThan(x) NotGreaterThan(x) greater than x GreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) NotGreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) greater than or equal to x LessThan(x) NotLessThan(x) less than x LessThanOrEqualTo(x) NotLessThanOrEqualTo(x) less than or equal to x Between(min).And(max) NotBetween(min).And(max) between min and max, both bounds included Passing the value directly, e.g. HasLength(10), is a shorthand for EqualTo. Comparing with null The expected value is nullable, e.g. to pass a value mapped from a property.
